## Term Project

Announced 2026-09-10 in lecture ([lec05](course-notes/lec05-2026-09-10-ipc-pipes-kernels-client-server.md)).
**Full spec (v1.0, 2026-08-03) is converted, section-for-section, in
[Term Project/term-project-spec.md](Term%20Project/Instructions/term-project-spec.md)** — read that before
answering any project question; this section is only the index. Standing question:
*"Who wants this, and why doesn't a phone app already solve it?"*

**The hard constraints, in one place** (spec §3, §10, §12, §13):
- Team of **exactly two**. One Raspberry Pi (40-pin header). Budget ~$50–80/team.
- **Two physically distinct sensors that cooperate** (fused / correlated / one shared pipeline
  whose behavior depends on both). Two demos stapled together does not count.
- **≥ 2 of the six "menu" mechanisms**, written by us, justified from the user's requirements,
  and measured: **A** kernel module/char driver · **B** interrupt-driven input vs. polling ·
  **C** `SCHED_FIFO`/`SCHED_RR` real-time path · **D** custom crash-consistent storage layer ·
  **E** multi-process + IPC + supervisor that survives any child dying · **F** high-rate no-drop
  SPSC/lock-free sampling pipeline.
- **The intelligence is ours:** no LLM, no cloud inference, no pretrained model at runtime (math
  primitives like an FFT are fine). "If a single threshold could do it, it isn't intelligence."
  Device must work with the network cable unplugged (LAN dashboard OK).
- **Systems core in C17/C23, `-Wall -Wextra -Werror` clean**; ASan/valgrind findings cap that
  component at 50% (same rule as HW1). Interface layer may be anything, but no graded mechanism
  may hide in it.
- **48-hour unattended soak** with raw logs: timestamped startup, ≥hourly heartbeat (liveness,
  RSS, event counts), ≥1 injected fault (unplug a sensor 10 min or `kill -9` a sensor process)
  showing detect → degrade → recover, orderly end. Soak + live demo run on live sensors; all
  other testing may use *labeled* replay.
- **A specific, nameable user with a specific problem.** Memos that fail the phone-app test get
  returned for revision (costs a week).
- **Claude Code required in the workflow, forbidden in the product.** Per partner: own clone, own
  sessions, own `.jsonl` transcripts copied out at *every* milestone (30-day purge!),
  `PROMPTLOG.md` (6–10 episodes incl. one review of the partner's work), `REFLECTION.md`.
  ≥ 40 meaningful commits, both partners well represented; a "final submission" commit pair =
  process grade of zero for both.
- **Grading (100 pts, 10% of course):** memo 5 · design doc 10 · checkpoint demo 10 · final
  system + soak 30 · evaluation report 15 (team) · transcripts 10 · demo-day defense 20
  (individual: line-level questions on own subsystem, one cross-boundary question, PROMPTLOG
  defense, a live solo modification). Staff **will** unplug a sensor mid-demo.

## Current Knowledge State

- **OS history:** generational view (vacuum tubes → transistors/batch → ICs/multiprogramming → PCs), why OSes live long (evolve in families rather than get rewritten), rough kernel codebase scale.
- **Hardware/memory hierarchy:** von Neumann architecture; registers & special registers (PC, SP, PSW); cache lines and hit/miss mechanics; the 4-level hierarchy table (registers/cache/main memory/disk) with size, access time, managed-by, backed-by; disk capacity history; the human-scaled latency comparison (why the CPU/disk speed gap matters to OS design); the "technology drives relative-performance cycles" theme (caches, assembly usage, etc. can become obsolete and un-obsolete as hardware ratios shift).
- **Kernel abstraction:** kernel vs. user mode as a 1-bit hardware distinction; the 3 minimum hardware requirements for isolation (privileged instructions, memory protection, timer interrupts); privileged instructions; memory-protection rationale (security *and* privacy); hardware timers and why the kernel can't detect infinite loops directly; mode transitions and their 3 triggers (interrupts = async, exceptions & system calls = sync/"trap"); system call mechanics and the "assume malicious parameters" defensive-programming principle; the interrupt vector table (x86: entries 0-31 exceptions, 32-255 interrupts, entry 64 = syscall handler); the 4 kernel-to-user transition triggers (new process, resume, switch, upcall).
- **Processes:** definition (execution of a program with restricted rights); multiprogramming vs. pseudoparallelism; process vs. program distinction; how a program becomes a process (executable image → kernel copies into memory → stack/heap set aside → needs a process ID); process memory layout (text/data/heap/stack); light intro to paging (pages, non-contiguous physical mapping — full mechanics not yet covered); process state transition diagram (new/ready/running/waiting/terminated); Process Control Block (PCB) contents and purpose; context switches and what makes them slow.
- **Process creation & lifecycle:** parent/child relationships, process trees, unique PIDs; `fork()` mechanics (copies parent's memory image, return value 0 in child vs. child-PID in parent, both processes resume right after the call); classic loop patterns (chain/fan/tree) from varying which process breaks out of a fork loop; `exec()` (destroys+replaces memory image, why fork-then-exec enables fd redirection); `wait()`/`waitpid()` and the 4 pid-sign meanings; Windows' `CreateProcess` (single-step creation+load, no fork/exec split, no real process hierarchy); process groups (pgid, group leader, signal delivery only within a group); termination types (voluntary: normal/error exit; involuntary: fatal error/killed); zombies and adoption by `init`.
- **Buffer overflows & security:** stack layout mechanics (local vars, saved frame pointer, return address; stack grows high→low); how an overflow can corrupt adjacent stack variables and the return address; the 1988 Morris Worm as a worked case study (trust-based spread via `rsh`/`sendmail` + a real buffer-overflow exploit in the `finger` daemon).
- **Shells, POSIX & IPC:** shell mechanics (fork-exec-wait loop, background processes with `&`, daemons); POSIX history and purpose (System V vs. BSD incompatibility → POSIX.1 1988 → Spec 1170 1994 → Austin Group 1998 → Single UNIX Spec v3 / IEEE 1003.1-2001 approved 2001-2002); independent vs. cooperating processes and why cooperation is useful; the two IPC mechanisms — shared memory (fast, no built-in synchronization) vs. message passing (kernel-mediated, slower, simpler); producer-consumer problem and the circular buffer (in/out indices, empty = `in==out`, full = `(in+1)%SIZE==out`, N-slot buffer holds N−1 usable elements); POSIX shared-memory API (`shmget`→`shmat`→use→`shmdt`/`shmctl`); message passing's three design axes (direct/indirect communication, blocking/non-blocking synchronization, zero/bounded/unbounded buffering); Windows XP LPC as a worked example of shared memory + message passing combined in one real system.
- **Pipes:** ordinary pipes (UNIX `pipe()`/`fd[0]`/`fd[1]`, inherited via `fork()`, close-unused-end idiom for EOF semantics; Windows anonymous pipes, not auto-inherited, unidirectional) vs. named pipes/FIFOs (no parent-child relationship needed, outlive the processes using them, `mkfifo()` on UNIX, full-duplex on Windows).
- **Kernel architecture:** monolithic kernels (tight module interdependency, used by Windows/macOS/Linux, portability challenges across ISAs and especially device drivers, the 60%-device-code/90%-driver-crash Linux statistic) vs. microkernels (minimal kernel, services as user-level processes communicating only via the microkernel, mechanism-vs-policy split, isolation-is-not-free performance cost, the Windows NT→XP monolithic drift as a real case study) vs. hybrid designs.
- **Client-server communication:** RPC (request/reply model, blocking calls, RPC daemon on a port, network failure modes — size limits/reordering/loss — and the XDR fix for big-endian/little-endian data representation, client/server stub architecture); distributed objects (RPC + inheritance, CORBA/RMI, IDL, ORB, GIOP/IIOP).
- **Threads:** why threads exist (shared address space vs. process isolation, 10-100x cheaper to create than processes, GUI responsiveness is a perceived-not-actual speedup); the process model split into resource-grouping vs. execution; per-process vs. per-thread resources (address space/heap/globals/files shared; PC/registers/stack/state unique per thread); no memory protection between threads (impossible + unnecessary, since one user owns all threads in a process); the 4 benefits of multithreading (responsiveness, resource sharing, economy, scalability); concurrency (single-core interleaving) vs. parallelism (multi-core simultaneity); user-level threads (thread table in user space, invisible to kernel, "jacket" functions managing blocking calls) vs. kernel-level threads (kernel-visible, more expensive, system-wide scheduling); the three thread models — many-to-one (no true concurrency, one blocking call blocks everything), one-to-one (true concurrency, per-thread kernel overhead, the dominant real-world model), many-to-many/two-level (tunable multiplexing); thread libraries (pthreads — `pthread_create`/`join`/`exit`/`cancel`/`detach`, returns non-zero error codes and does NOT set `errno` unlike `fork()`; Java threads — `Runnable`/`Thread`/`Executor`, `.start()`/`.join()`/`.interrupt()`; Win32 threads).
- **Synchronization (lec08–lec10):** race condition = outcome depends on the order of accesses (e.g. `counter++`/`counter--` are 3 machine steps each, so final value can be 4 or 6 instead of 5); critical section = code touching shared data, structure entry/critical/exit/remainder, a process may have several; **3 requirements** — mutual exclusion, progress (only non-remainder processes decide who enters, no indefinite postponement), bounded waiting; preemptive vs. nonpreemptive kernels; **Peterson's** (exactly 2 processes, `flag[2]` + `turn`, entry `flag[i]=TRUE; turn=j; while(flag[j]&&turn==j);`, no guarantees on modern hardware); hardware assists (disable interrupts, atomic `Swap`, `TestAndSet`, x86 `XCHG`) and the N-process TestAndSet with `waiting[]` that gets bounded wait in n−1 turns; **semaphores** (atomic `wait`/`signal`, binary = mutex, counting = N resources, busy-wait spinlock vs. blocking with wait queue + `wakeup`, negative value = number waiting), deadlock from opposite lock order, priority inversion + priority inheritance; classic problems — bounded buffer (`mutex=1, empty=n, full=0`), readers-writers (first problem: writers may starve; second: readers may starve; `readcount`/`mutex`/`wrt`), dining philosophers (simple semaphore solution deadlocks if all grab the same side); how semaphores get misused (swap order, wait-wait, omissions); **monitors** (ADT with automatic mutual exclusion, one process active, entry queue) and **condition variables** (`wait`/`signal`; signal with no waiter is lost, unlike a semaphore's persistent count; signal-and-wait vs. signal-and-continue), dining philosophers via monitor (`THINKING/HUNGRY/EATING`, `test()`), starvation still possible.
- **Atomic transactions (lec11):** all-or-nothing logical unit of work, commit vs. abort, rollback; write-ahead log (record = transaction, item, old value, new value; log written *before* data); undo/redo are idempotent; recovery rule (start without commit = undo, start + commit = redo); checkpoints shorten recovery (commit before checkpoint = no redo); conflict (same item + at least one write), conflict serializability, shared/exclusive locks, two-phase locking (growing/shrinking, deadlock possible), timestamp protocols (no deadlock, R/W-timestamps, reject + roll back on "from the future" accesses); Solaris adaptive mutex/turnstiles, Linux `preempt_count`/`atomic_t`/mutex.
- **CPU scheduling (lec12, NOT on midterm 1):** CPU-I/O burst cycle (I/O-bound = many short bursts, CPU-bound = few long), preemptive vs. nonpreemptive (needs timer), dispatcher + dispatch latency, criteria (utilization, throughput, turnaround, waiting, response), FCFS (convoy effect), SJF (optimal average wait only when all jobs arrive together), SRTF (starvation, pessimal variance), EWMA burst prediction `τ(n+1)=α·t(n)+(1−α)τ(n)`.
- **Not yet covered:** scheduling algorithms beyond FCFS/SJF (priority, round-robin, multilevel feedback queues, lottery, Linux CFS — previewed only), full virtual memory/paging details, file systems, I/O subsystems, deadlock as its own topic (only seen as examples inside synchronization), sockets/networking mechanics. Don't reach for these until they show up in a lecture.

# Progress log

Where the project stands, written so that either partner, or a fresh Claude Code session, can pick
up cold. **Read this after `CLAUDE.md` and before starting work.** Newest entry first. Facts and
evidence only; plans live in `DESIGN.md` and `docs/design-review.md`.

When you finish a chunk of work, add an entry at the top: date, who, what changed, how it was
verified, and what it leaves open.

---

## 2026-10-27 (evening) — M2 design document written (Liam)

Nick was unavailable, so Liam wrote `DESIGN.md` alone for the M2 deadline (2026-10-28, Canvas
date). The course handout was read in full and is kept locally only (`docs/CS370-TermProject.pdf`,
git-ignored).

### What changed

| Commit | What |
|---|---|
| `f85b220` | `.gitignore` the handout PDF |
| `4a75922` | DESIGN: architecture diagram with a rate on every arrow |
| `4deb2f6` | DESIGN: mechanism mapping. E: R-E1 (UNKNOWN within 60 s), R-E2 (≤ 10 s lost per crash). D: R-D1 (≤ 60 s lost per power cut), R-D2 (20/20 recoveries), R-D3 (≥ 180 days on 16 GB) |
| `584ac8b` | DESIGN: failure-mode table (13 rows, each with how to inject it) and storage |
| `32a55e8` | New [`record-and-ipc.md`](record-and-ipc.md): record layout, payloads, rate derivation, ring invariants, channels, supervision rules |
| `9fa7f0b` | DESIGN: constraints and evaluation plan (14 rows, each with a numeric target) |
| `b053730` | DESIGN: ownership, AI-use plan, trimmed to 5 pages |
| this commit | `CLAUDE.md`, hardware log, this entry |

### How it was verified

- On a CS department Linux machine (x86-64, gcc 16.1.0), **not the Pi**: `make` exit 0;
  `make test` 116 checks, 0 failed; `make asan` 116 checks, 0 failed; `make clean && make
  memcheck` 0 errors, no leaks.
- `DESIGN.md` is 5 pages rendered by pandoc → PDF (xelatex, 11 pt, 1-inch margins, US letter).
  The handout sets no format; this is the measure we used.
- `grep -rnE 'AF_INET|PF_INET|getaddrinfo|gethostbyname|curl|https?://' src/` prints nothing.

### Decisions marked "proposed (Liam), Nick to confirm" (‡ in DESIGN.md)

1. **Hub → storage:** `AF_UNIX SOCK_SEQPACKET`, one record per message. `stored` accepts
   `fusiond` and `dskyd` and stays the only writer. While `stored` is down, `fusiond` buffers 4096
   records (≈ 50 min), then drops the oldest and counts.
2. **Durability:** `write()` every 10 s or 64 records; `fsync()` every 60 s, at rotation and at
   shutdown; directory `fsync()` after creating a segment.
3. **Segments:** one per night, rotated at local noon (every 24 h of monotonic time when the clock
   is unsynced), 32 MB cap. No MANIFEST: recovery scans only the open segment.
4. **Retention:** raw 180 days, rollups forever; raw writes stop below 2 GB free.
5. **Torn header:** a 1–23-byte file with our segment name in our data directory is recreated; any
   other short file is still refused.
6. **`seq` per (source, run):** a new kind START (= 6) opens every run, carrying the run number
   from `dskyd`.
7. **Failures in records:** an I/O failure is a FAULT (the first, then ≤ 1 per 60 s); an
   implausible value is a SAMPLE without `VALID`.
8. **`source_id`s:** 0 reserved, 1 `skyd`, 2 `cloudd`, 3 `envd`, 4 `fusiond`, 5 `dskyd`,
   6 `stored`.
9. **Payloads:** Nick's SAMPLE table adopted as is; FEATURE, STATE, HEARTBEAT, FAULT and START
   added; new flag `CLOCK_UNSYNC` = bit 4. No layout change. See `record-and-ipc.md`.
10. **Analysis split:** Liam takes the classifier + state machine; Nick takes features,
    ephemeris and `dsq`.
11. **Evaluation targets in Nick's area:** row 2 (durable p99 ≤ 61 s), 10 (`fsync` sweep, ≤ 30
    MB/day written at 60 s), 11 (power cut 20/20, ≤ 60 s lost), 12 (ephemeris ≤ 0.1° sun, ≤ 0.5°
    moon).

### Decided in Liam's area (mechanism E)

Three sensor daemons share the bus; an I2C broker is the fallback if p99 interval jitter > 100 ms.
Shared-memory single-producer/single-consumer rings, chosen for decoupled lifetimes. One thread
per process. A hang is detected after 20 s of a silent liveness pipe. A "sensor absent" exit code
→ `DEAD` + re-probe every 60 s. Crash backoff 1 → 60 s; 5 crashes in 300 s → `DEAD`. systemd
supervises `dskyd`; children use `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG`. Hourly heartbeat; stderr → journald. No IP
sockets. With no RTC: `CLOCK_UNSYNC` flag and an UNKNOWN verdict.

### Hardware

- **Two kits.** `darksky.local` (Nick) is the device of record: soak, demo and every evaluation
  number. `starlight.local` (Liam: Pi $45 + sensors $32 = $77) is for development only. Team
  ≈ $145 against the handout's $50–80 guideline, before the unrecorded PSUs, SD cards, RTC and
  enclosure.
- DS3231 RTC: to be ordered.
- **No sensor wired on either kit.** "Both sensors electrically alive" was not met for M2; target
  2026-11-03 for hardware-log §1–5 on `darksky.local`.

### Open

- **Nick:** confirm or change items 1–11 above, then review the DESIGN.md diffs (that review is
  the PROMPTLOG cross-review episode).
- **Liam:** write up a review of Nick's `src/store/` and `src/common/` in `PROMPTLOG-liam.md`.
  Findings so far: a 1–23-byte file is refused forever (item 5 addresses it), no directory
  `fsync` after create, and `seq` resets on restart (item 6 addresses it).
- **Both:** copy out M2 transcripts to `transcripts/<name>/2026-10-27-m2/`.
- **Makefile bug, not fixed:** `make memcheck` straight after `make asan` runs valgrind on the
  ASan binary and crashes. Run `make clean` first. `vgcore.*` is also missing from `.gitignore`.
- **Docs that still contradict the design:**
  - README says the Pi isn't ordered and the project is at M0.
  - The BOM's Decisions section says Pi 4 2 GB, "buy Adafruit" and a 32 GB high-endurance card;
    we have 1 GB, clones and a standard 16 GB card. It also argues for both a narrow and a wide
    field of view.
  - `design-review.md` says the project can't work without an RTC.
  - `transcripts/README.md` names `liam/2026-09-23-m1/`; the folder is `m0-m1`.
- **Prices not recorded:** PSUs, SD cards, card reader (both kits).
- **Commits after this one:** 26 in total, Liam 9 (≈ 35 %).

---

# Transcripts

Raw Claude Code `.jsonl` session files, **per partner, per milestone.** These are a graded
deliverable (10 individual points each, spec §13) and committing them here is how they survive
the 30-day local purge.

## The rule

> "the raw `.jsonl` session files from `~/.claude/projects/`, copied in as-is. Not summarized.
> Not exported. Not retyped." — spec §10.4

Copy out at **every** milestone M1 through M5, covering work since the previous milestone.
This costs a minute and is the only way to guarantee the transcripts graded at M5 actually cover
the whole semester.

## Where they come from

Claude Code stores sessions per working directory:

```
~/.claude/projects/<path-with-dashes>/<session-id>.jsonl
```

For work done inside this repo the directory is:

```
~/.claude/projects/-Users-<you>-Desktop-CS-370-Term-Project-term-project/
```

To copy your sessions for a milestone:

```bash
mkdir -p transcripts/<your-name>/<date>-<milestone>
cp ~/.claude/projects/-Users-<you>-Desktop-CS-370-Term-Project-term-project/*.jsonl \
   transcripts/<your-name>/<date>-<milestone>/
```

## The 30-day purge

Local transcripts are deleted after 30 days by default, and this project spans more than 30 days.
Either copy out at every milestone (do this anyway) or raise the retention window:

```bash
# in ~/.claude/settings.json
{ "cleanupPeriodDays": 180 }
```

Losing Week-5 transcripts in Week 15 is a **foreseeable loss, and foreseeable losses are not
excused** (spec §10.4).

## Important: sessions are personal

Each partner works in **their own clone and their own Claude Code sessions**, and commits their
own transcripts. The five-level transcript scale is applied per partner, to that partner's own
sessions. Working in one shared login defeats this and costs **both** partners.

## Step 2: put the three sensors on the breadboard

**How a breadboard connects things:**

- **The long strips along the edges** (marked **+** red and **−** blue) are each connected along their whole length. These will carry power: **+ = 3.3 V** and **− = ground**.
  - If the red or blue line has a **break in the middle**, that strip is split into two halves. In that case, keep everything on one half.
- **The middle area** has numbered rows. In each numbered row, the 5 holes **a–e** are connected to each other, and the 5 holes **f–j** are connected to each other. The groove down the center separates the two sides.

**Now place the boards.** Push each sensor's pins in **down one lettered column**, so **every pin lands in its own numbered row**. For example, a 4-pin board goes in column `c`, rows 3, 4, 5 and 6.

⚠️ **Never put a board's pins across a single row**, like row 3 in columns a, b, c and d. That connects all its pins to each other.

A layout with space between the boards:

| Sensor | Pins | Rows (column `c`) |
|---|---|---|
| GY-906 (MLX90614) | 4 | 3–6 |
| GY-BME280 | 6 | 10–15 |
| TSL2591 | all its pins | 19 onward |

Leave **rows 27–30 empty**. Two of them become the shared data lines in Step 3.

Make sure **each pin still has at least one free hole beside it in the same row**, because that's where its wire will go. If a board covers those holes, flip it so its body sits over the other side.

Use the **4 male-to-female wires**: the socket end goes on the Pi's pin, and the pin end goes in the breadboard. The Pi stays **unplugged**.

|---|---|---|

Pin 1 is at the end of the header **farthest from the USB ports**, on the **inner row**. On the underside, its solder pad is square.

```

 inner row:               [ 1: 3.3V] [ 3: SDA ] [ 5: SCL ] ...
          (end farthest from USB)        → toward USB ports
```

| Pi pin | Breadboard |
|---|---|
| Pin 1 (3.3 V) | **+ red strip** |
| Pin 6 (GND) | **− blue strip** |
| Pin 3 (SDA) | **Row 28**, hole `a` |
| Pin 5 (SCL) | **Row 30**, hole `a` |

⚠️ **Nothing touches pins 2 or 4 (5 V).**

## Step 4: each sensor (male-to-male wires)

Each wire starts in a **free hole in that pin's row** and goes to the place listed.

**GY-906 (MLX90614): 4 wires**

| Sensor pin | Goes to |
|---|---|
| VIN | + strip |
| GND | − strip |
| SDA | row 28 |
| SCL | row 30 |

**GY-BME280: 6 wires**

| Sensor pin | Goes to |
|---|---|
| VCC | + strip |
| GND | − strip |
| SDA | row 28 |
| SCL | row 30 |
| CSB | **+ strip** (tells the chip to use I2C, the connection our code uses) |
| SDO | **− strip** (sets its address to `0x76`) |

**TSL2591: 4 wires**

| Sensor pin | Goes to |
|---|---|
| VIN (or VCC) | + strip |
| GND | − strip |
| SDA | row 28 |
| SCL | row 30 |
| INT, and 3Vo if it has one | **nothing**. Leave them empty |

That's 14 wires. Row 28 and row 30 each end up with 4 wires in them: one from the Pi plus one from each sensor.

Check these before plugging in:

- [ ] Nothing is on Pi pins 2 or 4.
- [ ] Pin 1 goes to **+** and pin 6 goes to **−**.
- [ ] Every sensor's VIN/VCC is on **+** and every GND is on **−**. No power and ground are swapped.
- [ ] Every SDA goes to row 28 and every SCL goes to row 30.
- [ ] No board has two pins in the same row.

|---|---|
| One address missing | That sensor's 4 wires |
| Nothing at all | The Pi's 4 wires; SDA and SCL may be swapped |
| `77` instead of `76` | The BME280's SDO wire |

content.text:
How to read the diagram:

- **The purple boxes are your sensors.** I drew them below the breadboard so you can read the pin labels. In real life each board sits **on** the breadboard, with its pins in row `c` and its body leaning over rows `d` and `e`. That leaves holes `a` and `b` free for the wires.
- **Every wire starts in row `a` of its pin's column**, so it's in the same strip as that pin.
- **Red** wires go up to the **+** strip and **gray** wires go to the **−** strip. The BME280's CSB is red and its SDO is gray.
- **Column 28 (teal) and column 30 (amber) each get 4 wires:** one from the Pi and one from each sensor. Where the 4 wires land in that column (`a` to `e`) doesn't matter, because the whole column is connected.
- **Wires crossing over each other is fine.** Jumper wires are insulated.
- **Your TSL2591's pins may be in a different order** than I drew. Match by the printed label, not by position. INT gets nothing.

When it's all wired, do the checklist from Step 5, plug in the Pi, and tell me it's on.

content.text:
That's normal. It's not a problem, and you don't need a new diagram. The 6th pin is almost certainly labeled **3Vo** or **3V3**. That pin is an **output**: the board's own regulator puts out 3.3 V on it. We don't need it.

**On the TSL2591, connect only these 4:**

| Pin | Goes to |
|---|---|
| VIN (or VCC) | + strip |
| GND | − strip |
| SDA | column 28 |
| SCL | column 30 |

**Leave these 2 empty:** INT and 3Vo/3V3.

One exception: if there's **no** VIN or VCC pin at all and the only power-sounding pin is `3V3`, use that one for power instead. If yours has a label I haven't mentioned, tell me what it says before you plug in the Pi.

With 6 pins, the board takes **rows 19–24** in column `c` instead of 19–23. Everything else in the diagram stays the same.

content.text:
Those numbers are **Pi pin numbers**, not columns or counts. Each line in that box reads "pin number, then what the pin does":

| In the box | Means |
|---|---|
| `1  3.3V` | Pi **pin 1** is 3.3 V power |
| `6  GND` | Pi **pin 6** is ground |
| `3  SDA` | Pi **pin 3** is SDA (data) |
| `5  SCL` | Pi **pin 5** is SCL (clock) |

They aren't in order in the box because I lined each one up with where its wire goes on the breadboard: power and ground at the top, SDA and SCL lower down.

On the Pi itself, the four are on the end farthest from the USB ports:

```
 outer row:  [2] [4] [6 GND]
 inner row:  [1 3.3V] [3 SDA] [5 SCL]
```

So three of your wires go on the first three inner-row pins (1, 3, 5), and the ground wire goes on pin 6, across from pin 5.

content.text:
Use your **4 male-to-female wires**. The **female end** (the socket) pushes straight down onto a Pi pin, and the **male end** goes into the breadboard. **Keep the Pi unplugged** while you do this.

## 1. Turn the Pi so you can count the pins

Lay the Pi flat, parts facing up. Turn it so the **row of 40 pins runs along the far edge**, away from you, with the **USB and ethernet ports on your right**. Then the pins you need are at the **left end**:

```
            far edge of the board
   [ 2 ] [ 4 ] [ 6 ] [ 8 ] ...    ← back row
   [ 1 ] [ 3 ] [ 5 ] [ 7 ] ...    ← front row (closer to you)
     ↑
  left end                          USB ports →
```

**To double-check pin 1:** flip the Pi over. Pin 1's solder pad on the underside is **square**, and all the others are round.

## 2. Connect the four wires

| Pi pin | Where it is | Breadboard end goes to |
|---|---|---|
| **Pin 1** (3.3 V) | front row, 1st from left | **+ strip** |
| **Pin 3** (SDA) | front row, 2nd from left | **column 28** (a free hole) |
| **Pin 5** (SCL) | front row, 3rd from left | **column 30** (a free hole) |
| **Pin 6** (GND) | back row, 3rd from left | **− strip** |

Tips:

- Push each socket **all the way down** until it stops. A half-on wire can look connected when it isn't.
- **Nothing goes on the first two back-row pins** (2 and 4). Those are 5 V.
- If your wires come in colors, use **red for pin 1** and **black for pin 6**. That makes the Step 5 check easier.

## 3. Then the Step 5 checklist, and power on

Go through the checklist from Step 5. Then plug in the Pi, wait about a minute, and tell me it's on.

Hold the Pi the way it's drawn: header along the **far edge**, USB ports on the **right**.

- **The pins with colored outlines** (1, 3, 5 and 6) are the four that get a wire. The color matches where that wire goes.
- **The two red pins (2 and 4) are 5 V.** Nothing touches them.

- **Columns 28 and 30 already have the three sensor wires** from the first diagram. The Pi's wire is the 4th wire in each column.

Before powering on, flip the Pi over once and check that the pin with the **square** solder pad has your red wire on it. That's pin 1.

content.text:
It isn't collecting any data yet. Nothing is running on the Pi that reads the sensors on its own.

What I did today was a **one-time check**: I asked each sensor "are you there, and what's your reading right now?" and then stopped. Those readings weren't saved anywhere on the Pi. The only copy is the one I pasted into your repo:

- **Today's readings:** [docs/hardware-log.md](docs/hardware-log.md), section 1 ("First identity checks and readings")

**Where the data will go once the system exists:**

| Piece | What it does | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Sensor programs (`skyd`, `cloudd`, `envd`) | Read the sensors every few seconds, nonstop | ❌ Not written yet (Liam's part, needed for M3) |
| Storage (`stored`) | Saves every reading as a 48-byte record in `data/seg-000001.dsm` on the Pi's SD card | ⚠️ The file writer works (your Step 3), but nothing sends it readings yet |
| Query tool (`dsq`) | Lets you look at the stored data, since `.dsm` files are binary and not human-readable | ❌ Not written yet (yours, per proposal #10) |

So your M3 checkpoint ("both sensors through the real pipeline into real storage") is when you'll first be able to open a folder on the Pi and see data piling up.

ssh -o BatchMode=yes nickmarechal@darksky.local 'G=/usr/sbin/i2cget; S=/usr/sbin/i2cset; date -Is
for r in $(seq 136 161) $(seq 225 231); do printf "cal %d %d\n" $r $($G -y 1 0x76 $r); done
$S -y 1 0x76 0xF2 0x01; $S -y 1 0x76 0xF4 0x25; sleep 0.1
for r in $(seq 247 254); do printf "dat %d %d\n" $r $($G -y 1 0x76 $r); done
printf "mlx ta %d\nmlx to %d\n" $($G -y 1 0x5a 0x06 w) $($G -y 1 0x5a 0x07 w)
$S -y 1 0x29 0xA1 0x10; $S -y 1 0x29 0xA0 0x03; sleep 0.25
printf "tsl c0 %d\ntsl c1 %d\n" $($G -y 1 0x29 0xB4 w) $($G -y 1 0x29 0xB6 w)
$S -y 1 0x29 0xA0 0x00; $S -y 1 0x29 0xA1 0x00' 2>&1 | python3 -I -c '
import sys
cal, dat, kv = {}, {}, {}
lines = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
print("Pi clock:", lines[0])
for ln in lines[1:]:
    p = ln.split()
    if len(p) != 3: continue
    if p[0] == "cal": cal[int(p[1])] = int(p[2])
    elif p[0] == "dat": dat[int(p[1])] = int(p[2])
    else: kv[p[0] + " " + p[1]] = int(p[2])
def u16(a): return cal[a] | cal[a+1] << 8
def s16(a): v = u16(a); return v - 65536 if v > 32767 else v
def s8(v): return v - 256 if v > 127 else v
T1, T2, T3 = u16(0x88), s16(0x8A), s16(0x8C)
P = [u16(0x8E)] + [s16(a) for a in range(0x90, 0xA0, 2)]
H1, H2, H3 = cal[0xA1], s16(0xE1), cal[0xE3]
H4 = (s8(cal[0xE4]) << 4) | (cal[0xE5] & 0x0F)
H5 = (s8(cal[0xE6]) << 4) | (cal[0xE5] >> 4)
H6 = s8(cal[0xE7])
adc_P = (dat[0xF7] << 12) | (dat[0xF8] << 4) | (dat[0xF9] >> 4)
adc_T = (dat[0xFA] << 12) | (dat[0xFB] << 4) | (dat[0xFC] >> 4)
adc_H = (dat[0xFD] << 8) | dat[0xFE]
v1 = (adc_T/16384.0 - T1/1024.0) * T2
v2 = ((adc_T/131072.0 - T1/8192.0) ** 2) * T3
tf = v1 + v2; T = tf / 5120.0
v1 = tf/2.0 - 64000.0; v2 = v1*v1*P[5]/32768.0; v2 += v1*P[4]*2.0; v2 = v2/4.0 + P[3]*65536.0
v1 = (P[2]*v1*v1/524288.0 + P[1]*v1)/524288.0; v1 = (1.0 + v1/32768.0)*P[0]
p = 1048576.0 - adc_P; p = (p - v2/4096.0)*6250.0/v1
v1 = P[8]*p*p/2147483648.0; v2 = p*P[7]/32768.0; p += (v1 + v2 + P[6])/16.0
h = tf - 76800.0
h = (adc_H - (H4*64.0 + H5/16384.0*h)) * (H2/65536.0*(1.0 + H6/67108864.0*h*(1.0 + H3/67108864.0*h)))
h = max(0.0, min(100.0, h*(1.0 - H1*h/524288.0)))
ta = kv["mlx ta"]*0.02 - 273.15; to = kv["mlx to"]*0.02 - 273.15
c0, c1 = kv["tsl c0"], kv["tsl c1"]
cpl = 100*25/408.0
lux = (c0 - c1)*(1 - c1/c0)/cpl if c0 else 0.0
print(f"BME280   air temp {T:6.2f} C   humidity {h:5.1f} %RH   pressure {p/100:7.1f} hPa   (raw T={adc_T} P={adc_P} H={adc_H})")
print(f"MLX90614 sensor   {ta:6.2f} C   pointed-at {to:6.2f} C   difference {ta-to:+.2f} C")
print(f"TSL2591  full {c0}  IR {c1}  (medium gain 25x, 100 ms)  ~{lux:.0f} lux (rough)")
'

Here's a live reading from your room, taken at 12:37 pm by the Pi's clock:

| Sensor | What it measured |
|---|---|
| **BME280** | Air **18.7 °C (65.6 °F)**, humidity **39.7 %**, pressure **845.6 hPa** |

**Three signs the readings are real:**

- **The pressure matches your elevation.** Fort Collins is about 1,500 m up, where normal air pressure is around 845 hPa. A broken sensor or a bad conversion wouldn't land that close.
- **Two different sensors agree on the temperature.** The BME280 says 18.69 °C and the MLX90614's own temperature is 18.79 °C, only 0.1 °C apart.
- **The IR difference is about 0.** That's right for a ceiling at room temperature. At night, pointed at a clear sky, that difference should jump to about **+20 to +40 °C**. That jump is the cloud signal the whole project is built on.

lastPrompt: whats the margin of error, our thermostate says 62, so there is a margin or erro,r unless the thermostate we have in the house is more inaccturate then the sensors

content.text:
Your thermostat says **62 °F (16.7 °C)** and the sensors say **65.6 °F (18.7 °C)**, a gap of **3.6 °F (2 °C)**. That's more than the sensors' stated error, but it doesn't necessarily mean either one is wrong.

**The official margins of error:**

| Device | Stated accuracy |
|---|---|
| BME280 (air temperature) | ±1 °C (about ±1.8 °F) |
| MLX90614 (its own temperature) | about ±0.5 °C |
| Typical home thermostat | about ±1–2 °F, sometimes worse |

Add those up and a gap of about 1–2 °C is within what the devices allow. So the gap is at the edge of normal error, not proof that something's broken.

**Likely reasons, most likely first:**

1. **Check whether 62 is the current temperature or the setting.** A lot of thermostats show the temperature you set (the target) in big numbers, and the actual room temperature smaller.
2. **They're measuring different spots.** The thermostat is on a wall somewhere else in the house. Temperatures differ by a couple of degrees between rooms, and between floor level and desk level.
3. **Heat near the breadboard.** The Pi's processor is at **36 °C**, and your laptop and your own body are nearby. Both sensors sit in that same warm spot, which is why they agree with each other. Agreeing with each other doesn't prove they're right about the room.

**How to actually find out:** put the Pi and breadboard right next to the thermostat for about 20 minutes and I'll take a reading every minute. If the gap shrinks to about 1 °F, the difference was location. If it stays at 3–4 °F, it's heat from the Pi.

**Does it matter for the project?** Barely for spotting clouds, since that signal is a 20–40 °C swing. It does matter for two finer readings:

- **The dew warning**, which triggers at a 1 °C margin.
- **Humidity.** A sensor 2 °C warmer than the air around it reads humidity about 10 % low.

That's why the design says the BME280 needs to sit away from the Pi in the final enclosure.

**Side note on the clock:** the Pi booted this morning with its clock **about 38 minutes behind**, and showed the right time once it reached the internet. That's exactly the no-clock-chip problem the RTC is meant to fix, and it showed up on its own here. That's useful evidence for your design doc.

# CS 370 — Operating Systems — Secondary Brain

This file is auto-loaded every session in this project. It is the master index and
evolving instruction set for acting as Nick's OS-knowledge partner this semester.
I update it every time new material is processed — that's the evolution mechanism.

## Workspace layout (do not rename)

- `Lectures Slides/` — raw PDFs Nick uploads (lecture slides, handouts). Source
  material only, never edited.
- `course-notes/` — one markdown file per lecture, written by Claude after reading
  the PDF. Filename pattern: `course-notes/lecXX-topic-slug.md`
  (e.g. `course-notes/lec01-intro-to-os.md`).
- `Homeworks/` — one folder per assignment, named `hw1`, `hw2`, `hw3`, etc. Each
  `hwN/` contains the instructions Nick drops in (PDF/doc/whatever) plus any work
  product Claude helps produce. Nick creates new `hwN` folders as assignments show up.
- `Term Project/` — the semester project (Nick's folder name, top level — not under
  `Homeworks/`). Holds the original spec PDF, its full markdown conversion
  `term-project-spec.md`, and the idea brainstorm — the thinking/notes side.
  - `Term Project/Instructions/` — spec PDF, `term-project-spec.md`, `brainstorm.md` (Nick moved
    these here 2026-09-23).
  - `Term Project/submissions/` — built submission tarballs (not tracked in the repo).
  - `Term Project/term-project/` — **the actual git repo** (created 2026-09-23, `main` branch).
    Team deliverables live here: team `CLAUDE.md`, `README.md`, `PROBLEM.md`, `Makefile`,

## Current Knowledge State

- **OS history:** generational view (vacuum tubes → transistors/batch → ICs/multiprogramming → PCs), why OSes live long (evolve in families rather than get rewritten), rough kernel codebase scale.
- **Hardware/memory hierarchy:** von Neumann architecture; registers & special registers (PC, SP, PSW); cache lines and hit/miss mechanics; the 4-level hierarchy table (registers/cache/main memory/disk) with size, access time, managed-by, backed-by; disk capacity history; the human-scaled latency comparison (why the CPU/disk speed gap matters to OS design); the "technology drives relative-performance cycles" theme (caches, assembly usage, etc. can become obsolete and un-obsolete as hardware ratios shift).
- **Kernel abstraction:** kernel vs. user mode as a 1-bit hardware distinction; the 3 minimum hardware requirements for isolation (privileged instructions, memory protection, timer interrupts); privileged instructions; memory-protection rationale (security *and* privacy); hardware timers and why the kernel can't detect infinite loops directly; mode transitions and their 3 triggers (interrupts = async, exceptions & system calls = sync/"trap"); system call mechanics and the "assume malicious parameters" defensive-programming principle; the interrupt vector table (x86: entries 0-31 exceptions, 32-255 interrupts, entry 64 = syscall handler); the 4 kernel-to-user transition triggers (new process, resume, switch, upcall).
- **Processes:** definition (execution of a program with restricted rights); multiprogramming vs. pseudoparallelism; process vs. program distinction; how a program becomes a process (executable image → kernel copies into memory → stack/heap set aside → needs a process ID); process memory layout (text/data/heap/stack); light intro to paging (pages, non-contiguous physical mapping — full mechanics not yet covered); process state transition diagram (new/ready/running/waiting/terminated); Process Control Block (PCB) contents and purpose; context switches and what makes them slow.
- **Process creation & lifecycle:** parent/child relationships, process trees, unique PIDs; `fork()` mechanics (copies parent's memory image, return value 0 in child vs. child-PID in parent, both processes resume right after the call); classic loop patterns (chain/fan/tree) from varying which process breaks out of a fork loop; `exec()` (destroys+replaces memory image, why fork-then-exec enables fd redirection); `wait()`/`waitpid()` and the 4 pid-sign meanings; Windows' `CreateProcess` (single-step creation+load, no fork/exec split, no real process hierarchy); process groups (pgid, group leader, signal delivery only within a group); termination types (voluntary: normal/error exit; involuntary: fatal error/killed); zombies and adoption by `init`.
- **Buffer overflows & security:** stack layout mechanics (local vars, saved frame pointer, return address; stack grows high→low); how an overflow can corrupt adjacent stack variables and the return address; the 1988 Morris Worm as a worked case study (trust-based spread via `rsh`/`sendmail` + a real buffer-overflow exploit in the `finger` daemon).
- **Shells, POSIX & IPC:** shell mechanics (fork-exec-wait loop, background processes with `&`, daemons); POSIX history and purpose (System V vs. BSD incompatibility → POSIX.1 1988 → Spec 1170 1994 → Austin Group 1998 → Single UNIX Spec v3 / IEEE 1003.1-2001 approved 2001-2002); independent vs. cooperating processes and why cooperation is useful; the two IPC mechanisms — shared memory (fast, no built-in synchronization) vs. message passing (kernel-mediated, slower, simpler); producer-consumer problem and the circular buffer (in/out indices, empty = `in==out`, full = `(in+1)%SIZE==out`, N-slot buffer holds N−1 usable elements); POSIX shared-memory API (`shmget`→`shmat`→use→`shmdt`/`shmctl`); message passing's three design axes (direct/indirect communication, blocking/non-blocking synchronization, zero/bounded/unbounded buffering); Windows XP LPC as a worked example of shared memory + message passing combined in one real system.
- **Pipes:** ordinary pipes (UNIX `pipe()`/`fd[0]`/`fd[1]`, inherited via `fork()`, close-unused-end idiom for EOF semantics; Windows anonymous pipes, not auto-inherited, unidirectional) vs. named pipes/FIFOs (no parent-child relationship needed, outlive the processes using them, `mkfifo()` on UNIX, full-duplex on Windows).
- **Kernel architecture:** monolithic kernels (tight module interdependency, used by Windows/macOS/Linux, portability challenges across ISAs and especially device drivers, the 60%-device-code/90%-driver-crash Linux statistic) vs. microkernels (minimal kernel, services as user-level processes communicating only via the microkernel, mechanism-vs-policy split, isolation-is-not-free performance cost, the Windows NT→XP monolithic drift as a real case study) vs. hybrid designs.
- **Client-server communication:** RPC (request/reply model, blocking calls, RPC daemon on a port, network failure modes — size limits/reordering/loss — and the XDR fix for big-endian/little-endian data representation, client/server stub architecture); distributed objects (RPC + inheritance, CORBA/RMI, IDL, ORB, GIOP/IIOP).
- **Threads:** why threads exist (shared address space vs. process isolation, 10-100x cheaper to create than processes, GUI responsiveness is a perceived-not-actual speedup); the process model split into resource-grouping vs. execution; per-process vs. per-thread resources (address space/heap/globals/files shared; PC/registers/stack/state unique per thread); no memory protection between threads (impossible + unnecessary, since one user owns all threads in a process); the 4 benefits of multithreading (responsiveness, resource sharing, economy, scalability); concurrency (single-core interleaving) vs. parallelism (multi-core simultaneity); user-level threads (thread table in user space, invisible to kernel, "jacket" functions managing blocking calls) vs. kernel-level threads (kernel-visible, more expensive, system-wide scheduling); the three thread models — many-to-one (no true concurrency, one blocking call blocks everything), one-to-one (true concurrency, per-thread kernel overhead, the dominant real-world model), many-to-many/two-level (tunable multiplexing); thread libraries (pthreads — `pthread_create`/`join`/`exit`/`cancel`/`detach`, returns non-zero error codes and does NOT set `errno` unlike `fork()`; Java threads — `Runnable`/`Thread`/`Executor`, `.start()`/`.join()`/`.interrupt()`; Win32 threads).
- **Synchronization (lec08–lec10):** race condition = outcome depends on the order of accesses (e.g. `counter++`/`counter--` are 3 machine steps each, so final value can be 4 or 6 instead of 5); critical section = code touching shared data, structure entry/critical/exit/remainder, a process may have several; **3 requirements** — mutual exclusion, progress (only non-remainder processes decide who enters, no indefinite postponement), bounded waiting; preemptive vs. nonpreemptive kernels; **Peterson's** (exactly 2 processes, `flag[2]` + `turn`, entry `flag[i]=TRUE; turn=j; while(flag[j]&&turn==j);`, no guarantees on modern hardware); hardware assists (disable interrupts, atomic `Swap`, `TestAndSet`, x86 `XCHG`) and the N-process TestAndSet with `waiting[]` that gets bounded wait in n−1 turns; **semaphores** (atomic `wait`/`signal`, binary = mutex, counting = N resources, busy-wait spinlock vs. blocking with wait queue + `wakeup`, negative value = number waiting), deadlock from opposite lock order, priority inversion + priority inheritance; classic problems — bounded buffer (`mutex=1, empty=n, full=0`), readers-writers (first problem: writers may starve; second: readers may starve; `readcount`/`mutex`/`wrt`), dining philosophers (simple semaphore solution deadlocks if all grab the same side); how semaphores get misused (swap order, wait-wait, omissions); **monitors** (ADT with automatic mutual exclusion, one process active, entry queue) and **condition variables** (`wait`/`signal`; signal with no waiter is lost, unlike a semaphore's persistent count; signal-and-wait vs. signal-and-continue), dining philosophers via monitor (`THINKING/HUNGRY/EATING`, `test()`), starvation still possible.
- **Atomic transactions (lec11):** all-or-nothing logical unit of work, commit vs. abort, rollback; write-ahead log (record = transaction, item, old value, new value; log written *before* data); undo/redo are idempotent; recovery rule (start without commit = undo, start + commit = redo); checkpoints shorten recovery (commit before checkpoint = no redo); conflict (same item + at least one write), conflict serializability, shared/exclusive locks, two-phase locking (growing/shrinking, deadlock possible), timestamp protocols (no deadlock, R/W-timestamps, reject + roll back on "from the future" accesses); Solaris adaptive mutex/turnstiles, Linux `preempt_count`/`atomic_t`/mutex.
- **CPU scheduling (lec12, NOT on midterm 1):** CPU-I/O burst cycle (I/O-bound = many short bursts, CPU-bound = few long), preemptive vs. nonpreemptive (needs timer), dispatcher + dispatch latency, criteria (utilization, throughput, turnaround, waiting, response), FCFS (convoy effect), SJF (optimal average wait only when all jobs arrive together), SRTF (starvation, pessimal variance), EWMA burst prediction `τ(n+1)=α·t(n)+(1−α)τ(n)`.
- **Not yet covered:** scheduling algorithms beyond FCFS/SJF (priority, round-robin, multilevel feedback queues, lottery, Linux CFS — previewed only), full virtual memory/paging details, file systems, I/O subsystems, deadlock as its own topic (only seen as examples inside synchronization), sockets/networking mechanics. Don't reach for these until they show up in a lecture.

**The hard constraints, in one place** (spec §3, §10, §12, §13):
- Team of **exactly two**. One Raspberry Pi (40-pin header). Budget ~$50–80/team.
- **Two physically distinct sensors that cooperate** (fused / correlated / one shared pipeline
  whose behavior depends on both). Two demos stapled together does not count.
- **≥ 2 of the six "menu" mechanisms**, written by us, justified from the user's requirements,
  and measured: **A** kernel module/char driver · **B** interrupt-driven input vs. polling ·
  **C** `SCHED_FIFO`/`SCHED_RR` real-time path · **D** custom crash-consistent storage layer ·

## Current Knowledge State

- **OS history:** generational view (vacuum tubes → transistors/batch → ICs/multiprogramming → PCs), why OSes live long (evolve in families rather than get rewritten), rough kernel codebase scale.
- **Hardware/memory hierarchy:** von Neumann architecture; registers & special registers (PC, SP, PSW); cache lines and hit/miss mechanics; the 4-level hierarchy table (registers/cache/main memory/disk) with size, access time, managed-by, backed-by; disk capacity history; the human-scaled latency comparison (why the CPU/disk speed gap matters to OS design); the "technology drives relative-performance cycles" theme (caches, assembly usage, etc. can become obsolete and un-obsolete as hardware ratios shift).
- **Kernel abstraction:** kernel vs. user mode as a 1-bit hardware distinction; the 3 minimum hardware requirements for isolation (privileged instructions, memory protection, timer interrupts); privileged instructions; memory-protection rationale (security *and* privacy); hardware timers and why the kernel can't detect infinite loops directly; mode transitions and their 3 triggers (interrupts = async, exceptions & system calls = sync/"trap"); system call mechanics and the "assume malicious parameters" defensive-programming principle; the interrupt vector table (x86: entries 0-31 exceptions, 32-255 interrupts, entry 64 = syscall handler); the 4 kernel-to-user transition triggers (new process, resume, switch, upcall).
- **Processes:** definition (execution of a program with restricted rights); multiprogramming vs. pseudoparallelism; process vs. program distinction; how a program becomes a process (executable image → kernel copies into memory → stack/heap set aside → needs a process ID); process memory layout (text/data/heap/stack); light intro to paging (pages, non-contiguous physical mapping — full mechanics not yet covered); process state transition diagram (new/ready/running/waiting/terminated); Process Control Block (PCB) contents and purpose; context switches and what makes them slow.
- **Process creation & lifecycle:** parent/child relationships, process trees, unique PIDs; `fork()` mechanics (copies parent's memory image, return value 0 in child vs. child-PID in parent, both processes resume right after the call); classic loop patterns (chain/fan/tree) from varying which process breaks out of a fork loop; `exec()` (destroys+replaces memory image, why fork-then-exec enables fd redirection); `wait()`/`waitpid()` and the 4 pid-sign meanings; Windows' `CreateProcess` (single-step creation+load, no fork/exec split, no real process hierarchy); process groups (pgid, group leader, signal delivery only within a group); termination types (voluntary: normal/error exit; involuntary: fatal error/killed); zombies and adoption by `init`.
- **Buffer overflows & security:** stack layout mechanics (local vars, saved frame pointer, return address; stack grows high→low); how an overflow can corrupt adjacent stack variables and the return address; the 1988 Morris Worm as a worked case study (trust-based spread via `rsh`/`sendmail` + a real buffer-overflow exploit in the `finger` daemon).
- **Shells, POSIX & IPC:** shell mechanics (fork-exec-wait loop, background processes with `&`, daemons); POSIX history and purpose (System V vs. BSD incompatibility → POSIX.1 1988 → Spec 1170 1994 → Austin Group 1998 → Single UNIX Spec v3 / IEEE 1003.1-2001 approved 2001-2002); independent vs. cooperating processes and why cooperation is useful; the two IPC mechanisms — shared memory (fast, no built-in synchronization) vs. message passing (kernel-mediated, slower, simpler); producer-consumer problem and the circular buffer (in/out indices, empty = `in==out`, full = `(in+1)%SIZE==out`, N-slot buffer holds N−1 usable elements); POSIX shared-memory API (`shmget`→`shmat`→use→`shmdt`/`shmctl`); message passing's three design axes (direct/indirect communication, blocking/non-blocking synchronization, zero/bounded/unbounded buffering); Windows XP LPC as a worked example of shared memory + message passing combined in one real system.
- **Pipes:** ordinary pipes (UNIX `pipe()`/`fd[0]`/`fd[1]`, inherited via `fork()`, close-unused-end idiom for EOF semantics; Windows anonymous pipes, not auto-inherited, unidirectional) vs. named pipes/FIFOs (no parent-child relationship needed, outlive the processes using them, `mkfifo()` on UNIX, full-duplex on Windows).
- **Kernel architecture:** monolithic kernels (tight module interdependency, used by Windows/macOS/Linux, portability challenges across ISAs and especially device drivers, the 60%-device-code/90%-driver-crash Linux statistic) vs. microkernels (minimal kernel, services as user-level processes communicating only via the microkernel, mechanism-vs-policy split, isolation-is-not-free performance cost, the Windows NT→XP monolithic drift as a real case study) vs. hybrid designs.
- **Client-server communication:** RPC (request/reply model, blocking calls, RPC daemon on a port, network failure modes — size limits/reordering/loss — and the XDR fix for big-endian/little-endian data representation, client/server stub architecture); distributed objects (RPC + inheritance, CORBA/RMI, IDL, ORB, GIOP/IIOP).
- **Threads:** why threads exist (shared address space vs. process isolation, 10-100x cheaper to create than processes, GUI responsiveness is a perceived-not-actual speedup); the process model split into resource-grouping vs. execution; per-process vs. per-thread resources (address space/heap/globals/files shared; PC/registers/stack/state unique per thread); no memory protection between threads (impossible + unnecessary, since one user owns all threads in a process); the 4 benefits of multithreading (responsiveness, resource sharing, economy, scalability); concurrency (single-core interleaving) vs. parallelism (multi-core simultaneity); user-level threads (thread table in user space, invisible to kernel, "jacket" functions managing blocking calls) vs. kernel-level threads (kernel-visible, more expensive, system-wide scheduling); the three thread models — many-to-one (no true concurrency, one blocking call blocks everything), one-to-one (true concurrency, per-thread kernel overhead, the dominant real-world model), many-to-many/two-level (tunable multiplexing); thread libraries (pthreads — `pthread_create`/`join`/`exit`/`cancel`/`detach`, returns non-zero error codes and does NOT set `errno` unlike `fork()`; Java threads — `Runnable`/`Thread`/`Executor`, `.start()`/`.join()`/`.interrupt()`; Win32 threads).
- **Synchronization (lec08–lec10):** race condition = outcome depends on the order of accesses (e.g. `counter++`/`counter--` are 3 machine steps each, so final value can be 4 or 6 instead of 5); critical section = code touching shared data, structure entry/critical/exit/remainder, a process may have several; **3 requirements** — mutual exclusion, progress (only non-remainder processes decide who enters, no indefinite postponement), bounded waiting; preemptive vs. nonpreemptive kernels; **Peterson's** (exactly 2 processes, `flag[2]` + `turn`, entry `flag[i]=TRUE; turn=j; while(flag[j]&&turn==j);`, no guarantees on modern hardware); hardware assists (disable interrupts, atomic `Swap`, `TestAndSet`, x86 `XCHG`) and the N-process TestAndSet with `waiting[]` that gets bounded wait in n−1 turns; **semaphores** (atomic `wait`/`signal`, binary = mutex, counting = N resources, busy-wait spinlock vs. blocking with wait queue + `wakeup`, negative value = number waiting), deadlock from opposite lock order, priority inversion + priority inheritance; classic problems — bounded buffer (`mutex=1, empty=n, full=0`), readers-writers (first problem: writers may starve; second: readers may starve; `readcount`/`mutex`/`wrt`), dining philosophers (simple semaphore solution deadlocks if all grab the same side); how semaphores get misused (swap order, wait-wait, omissions); **monitors** (ADT with automatic mutual exclusion, one process active, entry queue) and **condition variables** (`wait`/`signal`; signal with no waiter is lost, unlike a semaphore's persistent count; signal-and-wait vs. signal-and-continue), dining philosophers via monitor (`THINKING/HUNGRY/EATING`, `test()`), starvation still possible.
- **Atomic transactions (lec11):** all-or-nothing logical unit of work, commit vs. abort, rollback; write-ahead log (record = transaction, item, old value, new value; log written *before* data); undo/redo are idempotent; recovery rule (start without commit = undo, start + commit = redo); checkpoints shorten recovery (commit before checkpoint = no redo); conflict (same item + at least one write), conflict serializability, shared/exclusive locks, two-phase locking (growing/shrinking, deadlock possible), timestamp protocols (no deadlock, R/W-timestamps, reject + roll back on "from the future" accesses); Solaris adaptive mutex/turnstiles, Linux `preempt_count`/`atomic_t`/mutex.
- **CPU scheduling (lec12, NOT on midterm 1):** CPU-I/O burst cycle (I/O-bound = many short bursts, CPU-bound = few long), preemptive vs. nonpreemptive (needs timer), dispatcher + dispatch latency, criteria (utilization, throughput, turnaround, waiting, response), FCFS (convoy effect), SJF (optimal average wait only when all jobs arrive together), SRTF (starvation, pessimal variance), EWMA burst prediction `τ(n+1)=α·t(n)+(1−α)τ(n)`.
- **Not yet covered:** scheduling algorithms beyond FCFS/SJF (priority, round-robin, multilevel feedback queues, lottery, Linux CFS — previewed only), full virtual memory/paging details, file systems, I/O subsystems, deadlock as its own topic (only seen as examples inside synchronization), sockets/networking mechanics. Don't reach for these until they show up in a lecture.

# term-project: team rules

Team law for CS 370 (Colorado State University, Prof. Shrideep Pallickara), Fall 2026.
Both partners maintain this file. Claude Code reads it every session, so **a constraint that
lives only in one partner's head protects nothing.**

This file is self-contained on purpose: a teammate who clones only this repo has everything
they need. (Nick has a separate personal course-notes folder one level up; that is not team law
and is not required to work in this repo.)

---

## Project status (update this as things get decided)

- **Idea: LOCKED — Dark Sky Monitor.** An offline device that measures sky brightness and cloud
  cover at one site and grades the night GOOD / MARGINAL / POOR / UNKNOWN with the evidence behind
  the verdict. Full design review in [`docs/design-review.md`](docs/design-review.md).
- **Team:** Nick Marechal + Liam Sagal.
- **Where we left off: [`docs/progress-log.md`](docs/progress-log.md). Read it first.** Newest
  entry on top: milestone position, what code exists and what it guarantees, the shared record
  contract, and the open work. Add an entry there when you finish a chunk of work.
- **Hardware: two kits.** **`darksky.local`** (Nick: Pi 4 Model B **1 GB** + TSL2591 + MLX90614
  **3.3 V** + BME280; arrived 2026-10-13, set up headless 2026-10-27, I2C on, power `0x0`) is the
  **device of record**: the soak, the demo and every evaluation number come only from it.
  **`starlight.local`** (Liam's dev Pi + the same three sensors) is for parallel development only.
  **`darksky.local`: all three sensors wired and answering 2026-10-28** (`0x29`, `0x5a`, `0x76`;
  BME280 genuine). `starlight.local` not wired. DS3231 RTC to be ordered; until it is fitted the Pi
  takes real time from the network at boot. Enclosure still unbought. See
  [`docs/hardware-log.md`](docs/hardware-log.md) and [`docs/bill-of-materials.md`](docs/bill-of-materials.md).
- **Mechanisms: D** (crash-consistent storage) **+ E** (multiprocess + IPC + supervisor). C and F
  were considered and rejected — at 0.1–1 Hz sampling neither is justified, and being able to say
  why is a stronger defense answer than bolting them on.
- **Design: `DESIGN.md` M2 written 2026-10-27 (Liam).** The decisions in Nick's area (listed in
  the 2026-10-27 M2 entry of [`docs/progress-log.md`](docs/progress-log.md)) were confirmed by
  Nick on 2026-10-28. Values marked (a) are datasheet assumptions,
  not measurements. Record, IPC and supervision detail: [`docs/record-and-ipc.md`](docs/record-and-ipc.md).
- **Next action:** finish hardware-log §3–5 on `darksky.local` (§1–2 done 2026-10-28, which met
  M2's "both sensors electrically alive"). Step 4 (acrylic vs. LDPE film in front of the MLX90614) tests
  the largest hardware unknown in the project.
- **Open gap:** the problem memo names an archetype, not a named individual. Outreach to the
  Northern Colorado Astronomical Society / CSU astronomy faculty still pending.

## Commands

- Build: `make`            Deploy to Pi: `make deploy PI=pi@<host>`
- Tests: `make test`       Sanitizers: `make asan`      Valgrind: `make memcheck`
- Soak sanity: `make soakcheck` (1-hour miniature of the 48h run)
- **A change is DONE only when build, test, and asan pass. Show the output.**

Targets exist and run today; several are no-ops until there is source to build. Do not let a
target silently become a lie — if it stops doing what its name says, fix it or rename it.

## Hard constraints (graded — spec §3.3, §3.4)

- The PRODUCT makes **no network calls except serving its own LAN interface**. No LLM APIs, no
  cloud inference, no pretrained models, no external weather/data APIs at runtime. The device
  must work with the network cable unplugged. The intelligence in `analysis/` is ours. A grader
  must be able to confirm this in one minute by reading the source tree.
  - Public data (NWS, USGS, etc.) may be used **only** as an offline ground-truth comparison
    while writing the evaluation report — never called from the device's own code.
- Every daemon must be **supervisable**: clean exit codes, no orphaned fds across restart,
  heartbeat within 60s of start.
- Every allocation checked; every syscall's error path handled and logged. The 48-hour soak is
  the test suite of last resort.
- **NEVER weaken, skip, or delete a test to make the suite pass.**
- Replayed or synthesized data is **labeled as such everywhere it appears** — in logs, in the
  report, in the demo. The 48h soak and the live demo run on live sensors.

## Style

- Systems core: **C17, `-Wall -Wextra -Werror`, no VLAs.** `goto`-cleanup for multi-resource
  functions. ASan/valgrind findings cap that component's score at 50%, so they are bugs, not
  warnings.
- Python permitted only under `tools/` and `ui/`. **No graded mechanism may live there.**
- Smallest diff that passes. Do not refactor unrelated code.

## Ownership

Ownership means **first authorship and answerability at the defense**, not exclusivity. Each
partner is individually examined on their own subsystems plus one question from across the
boundary.

- **Nick:** `src/common/` (record format + CRC — owned by storage, used by everyone) and
  `src/store/` — mechanism **D**, the crash-consistent storage layer.
- **Liam (confirmed by Liam 2026-10-27):** `src/super/`, `src/sensors/`, and the IPC — mechanism
  **E**: the supervisor (`dskyd`), the sensor daemons, the shm rings, sockets and pipes, and
  `fusiond`'s ring-draining loop. All Linux-only I2C code lives in `src/sensors/`, so everything
  else builds and tests on a Mac.
- **Analysis and query CLI (proposed by Liam, confirmed by Nick 2026-10-28):** Liam: classifier +
  state machine. Nick: features, ephemeris, and the `dsq` query CLI.
- The agent edits outside the current session owner's area only when told explicitly whose
  session this is.

## Workflow (spec §10, Assignment 0's nine steps apply verbatim)

- Multi-file or algorithmic change: **plan first, wait for approval.** No code in the first pass.
- **Hardware bugs: paste real evidence** — `dmesg`, timing captures, `/proc/interrupts`, logic
  analyzer output. Never propose or accept a fix derived from a verbal description of a sensor
  problem. The agent will confidently reason about a sensor it has never met and be wrong in
  ways only an instrument catches.
- Commit only from a green state; message format `M<n>: <what>`.
- **≥ 40 meaningful commits** across the project, both partners well represented. A pair of
  "final submission" commits is an automatic process grade of **zero, for both partners.**
- Each partner works in **their own clone and their own Claude Code sessions.** Working in one
  shared login defeats the per-partner transcript grading and costs both of you.
- Every milestone's diffs get **two reviews**: a fresh-context agent review and a human review
  by the partner who did not write the code. Each partner's `PROMPTLOG.md` must record at least
  one review of the other's work.

## Transcript discipline (do not skip — spec §6, §10.4)

At **every** milestone M1–M5, each partner copies their raw `.jsonl` sessions from
`~/.claude/projects/<project-dir>/` into `transcripts/<partner>/`. As-is. Not summarized, not
exported, not retyped. See `transcripts/README.md`.

Local transcripts purge after 30 days by default and this project spans more than 30 days.
Losing Week-5 transcripts in Week 15 is a foreseeable loss, and foreseeable losses are not
excused.

Hey Liam, here's where I'm at on the term project, and a piece you can take tonight that doesn't need any hardware.

**What I've done**
- Pi is set up (headless, SSH, I2C on, power checks out). I'm wiring the sensors on the breadboard tonight for the M2 "sensors electrically alive" part.
- Storage side (mechanism D): CRC-32, the 48-byte record format every process will use, and an append-only store file that refuses bad records and stops cleanly after a failed write. 116 tests, all passing, sanitizers clean, and valgrind clean on the Pi.
- Wrote everything up in the repo so your Claude has the full picture.

**To get caught up**
1. `git pull`
2. Read `docs/progress-log.md`. `CLAUDE.md` points your Claude to it automatically, but it's worth reading yourself too. It has where every milestone stands, what the code guarantees, the record format rules, and the open work.

**A piece you could take tonight: the sensor-reading code in `src/sensors/`** (your area on the ownership map). None of it needs the sensors plugged in to start:
- **Conversion functions first.** These turn raw register bytes into real units (temperatures, humidity, pressure, light counts). They're plain math with no I/O, so you can write tests for them right now using the worked examples in each datasheet. The MLX90614 is the quickest one to start with, and the BME280 has the most math to get right.
- **Then the Linux I2C layer**: open `/dev/i2c-1` and read the registers.
- **Then a small program that reads all three sensors once and prints the values.** That's our M2 proof that the sensors are alive, and it turns into the sensor processes at M3.

The progress log has the register addresses and the gotchas for each chip. Check them against the datasheets, since they came from memory, not from a PDF.

**A few things to keep in mind**
- Use your own clone and your own Claude sessions. Transcripts are graded per person.
- Small commits with the `M2: <what>` format. Almost all the commits so far are mine, and we need at least 40 total with both of us well represented.
- I develop on a Mac, so Linux-only code (anything with `<linux/i2c-dev.h>`) can't go straight into the Makefile's `SRC` list or it breaks my build. The progress log explains the fix.
- The table of which sensor value goes in which record slot is only a proposal. If you'd do it differently, change it and tell me.
- At some point, review my store code (`src/store/`) for your PROMPTLOG. The spec requires each of us to review the other's work.
- Also confirm your side of the ownership map in `CLAUDE.md`. It still says "proposed."

Once my sensors are wired tonight I'll put the `i2cdetect` output in `docs/hardware-log.md`. Then we can run your program on my Pi.

# Plan: baseline storage-layer code (mechanism D) before the hardware arrives

## Context

The parts are in transit. Nick wants code down now. The storage layer needs no sensors at all —
it is files, bytes, and checksums — so it can be built and fully tested on the Mac today.

Nick chose to **own storage (mechanism D)**. Liam takes the supervisor + IPC (mechanism E) and the
sensor daemons. Whatever is written in Nick's sessions is his to defend line-by-line at the demo, so
every step is small enough to explain back without notes.

Storage is also the right thing to build first for a structural reason: the **record format is the
thing every other part of the system uses.** Liam's sensor daemons produce records, the IPC moves
records, the classifier reads records. Building it first unblocks him.

It also maps directly onto **lec11** (atomic transactions): the recovery step below *is* a
write-ahead-log recovery — scan forward, keep what verifies, discard the torn tail — and the
"recovery is idempotent" test is the same property as idempotent undo/redo.

The design being implemented is already written: `docs/design-review.md` §8 (data model) and §9
(storage). This plan breaks it into steps.

## How we work each step

One step at a time. Each step ends only when all of these are true:

1. Tests written **first**, and they fail for the right reason.
2. Code written; `make test` green.
3. `make asan` clean — zero AddressSanitizer / UBSan findings (findings cap the component at 50%).
4. Nick can explain the step in his own words and writes his own comments where he wants them.
5. Diff shown; **Nick runs the commit** (or says "you run it"), format `M3: <what>`.

Then stop and wait before starting the next step.

## Layout

Directory per owner, so a grader can read the ownership map straight off the tree (this is how
the spec's own sample `CLAUDE.md` does it):

```
src/common/   crc32.{c,h}  record.{c,h}   storage-owned (Nick), shared by everyone
src/store/    store.{c,h}                 Nick — mechanism D
src/super/    (Liam, later)               mechanism E
src/sensors/  (Liam, later)               Linux-only I2C code lives ONLY here
tests/        check.h  test_main.c  test_crc32.c  test_record.c  test_store.c
```

Keeping all Linux-only I2C code inside `src/sensors/` is what lets everything else build and test
on a Mac.

## Steps

### Step 0 — Build skeleton + ownership map
- **`Makefile`**: restructure to Nick's HW2 pattern (explicit `SRC` / `TSRC` lists, one test
  binary `build/test_all`, `asan: CFLAGS += …; asan: clean test`). Keep `soakcheck`, `deploy`,
  `help`. Keep the "no lying targets" rule: `all` builds what it says.
- Add **`-D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L`** to `CFLAGS`. Without it, `-std=c17` on the Pi's glibc hides
  `fsync`/`ftruncate`/`pread`/`clock_gettime`, and `-Werror` fails — but it compiles fine on the
  Mac, so this bug would only appear the day the code first reaches the Pi.
- **`tests/check.h`**: the `CHECK(cond, ...)` macro + failure counter — same shape as HW2's
  `tests/test_rbtree.c`, so it's already familiar. `test_main.c` runs every suite, prints totals,
  exits non-zero on any failure.
- **Team `CLAUDE.md` ownership section**: Nick = `src/common`, `src/store`. Liam = `src/super`,
  `src/sensors`, IPC (**marked proposed until Liam confirms**). Analysis/classifier: TBD together.
- Done when: `make`, `make test`, `make asan` all run and pass with an empty test suite.

### Step 1 — CRC-32
- `src/common/crc32.{c,h}`: standard CRC-32 (IEEE, reflected poly `0xEDB88320`), ~15 lines.
- **Why our own instead of zlib's `crc32()`:** no dependency, tiny, and explainable at the
  defense. zlib would also be acceptable — it's a math primitive, which the spec allows.
- **Tests first:** the standard check value — `crc32("123456789") == 0xCBF43926`. Empty input.
  One flipped bit changes the result.

### Step 2 — The record format
- `src/common/record.{c,h}`: `struct dsm_record`, exactly as in design-review §8 (48 bytes).
  Enums for `kind` (SAMPLE / FEATURE / STATE / HEARTBEAT / FAULT) and `flags` (VALID / STALE /
  **SYNTHETIC** / CALIBRATING).
- `record_seal()` computes the CRC over everything before the `crc32` field and stores it.
  `record_valid()` recomputes and compares.
- Compile-time guards: `_Static_assert` that the size is 48, that `crc32` sits at offset 44, and
  that the host is little-endian (the Pi and Apple Silicon both are). If anyone edits the struct
  and changes the layout, the build fails instead of the data silently corrupting.
- **Design choice to defend:** we write the struct's bytes straight to disk. The alternative is
  serializing field-by-field, which is more portable but more code. The static asserts are what
  make the simple version safe.
- **Tests first:** a sealed record validates; **flipping any one of its 48 bytes** makes it
  invalid (loop over all 48).

### Step 3 — Append-only writer
- `src/store/store.{c,h}`: `store_open(path)`, `store_append(s, &rec)`, `store_close(s)`.
- Each file starts with a small **header** (magic `"DSKY"`, schema version, record size, creation
  time, its own CRC). A wrong header means "not our file" → refuse it, never truncate it.
- `goto`-cleanup on every multi-resource path (team style rule).
- **Tests first:** write N records, reopen, read them all back, same order, all valid.

### Step 4 — Crash recovery by truncation (the core of mechanism D)
- `store_recover(path, &kept, &discarded_bytes)`: scan forward from the header, validate each
  48-byte record, stop at the first short or bad one, `ftruncate` there, report what was dropped.
- **Design choice to defend:** truncate at the *first* bad record even if later ones look fine.
  In an append-only log, anything after a corrupt record is suspect, and it's the simplest rule to
  prove correct. Alternative: skip bad records and keep scanning — more data kept, harder to trust.
- **Tests first — these simulate a power cut:**
  - **Torn tail:** 10 records + a half-written 11th → keeps 10, discards the partial bytes.
  - **Corrupt middle:** one flipped byte in record 6 → keeps 5, truncates from 6.
  - **Idempotent:** recovery on a clean file changes nothing; running it twice = running it once.
  - Empty file / header-only file.
  - **Foreign file** (bad magic) → refuses, file untouched.

### Step 5 — Write batching + fsync policy
- Buffer K records in memory, one `write()` per flush. `fsync()` every N flushes and on close.
- **K and N are the knobs for the evaluation's fsync experiment** (design-review §13): data-loss
  window vs. write amplification vs. SD wear. Counters in the store struct record how many
  `write()` and `fsync()` calls happened, so the tests and the later experiment can measure them.
- **Tests first:** nothing reaches disk before a flush; close flushes; K appends cost one
  `write()`.

### Not in this plan (named so they're not forgotten)
Segment rotation + `MANIFEST`, nightly rollups, the query CLI, the free-space guard. Next round.

## Files

- Modified: `Makefile`, `CLAUDE.md` (ownership section)
- New: `src/common/crc32.{c,h}`, `src/common/record.{c,h}`, `src/store/store.{c,h}`,
  `tests/check.h`, `tests/test_main.c`, `tests/test_crc32.c`, `tests/test_record.c`,
  `tests/test_store.c`
- Reused: the `CHECK` macro pattern from Nick's HW2 `tests/test_rbtree.c`; the existing
  `Makefile` targets `soakcheck`, `deploy`, `help`; the struct from `docs/design-review.md` §8.

## Verification

- `make` — clean under `-std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror`.
- `make test` — every suite passes; non-zero exit on any failure.
- `make asan` — zero ASan/UBSan findings.
- CRC matches the published check value `0xCBF43926`.
- Recovery tests reproduce a torn write and a mid-file corruption and show exact bytes discarded.
- **First time the code reaches the Pi:** `make test` and `make memcheck` there (valgrind isn't
  available on the Mac), plus confirm the `_POSIX_C_SOURCE` fix holds under glibc.
- Note for later: on macOS `fsync` doesn't force data all the way to the drive the way it does
  on Linux, so **the real fsync timing experiment must run on the Pi**, not the Mac. The logic
  tests here are unaffected.

definition.name: SearchPlugins
definition.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

keywords.description: Keyword phrases describing the user's intent.

definition.name: SuggestPluginInstall
definition.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

contextLabel.description: Short header tying the suggestion to the user request.
