tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

text.description: For 'text': the string to type.

name.description: For 'button': hardware button to press.

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. content.content:
## 6 Milestones

The project runs from **Week 3 through demo week**. Milestones are due at the **end of the listed
week**; each is graded, and each exists to make a specific late-semester disaster impossible.

| Milestone | Deliverable | Week | Est. team hours |
|---|---|---|---|
| **M0** | Team formed; hardware ordered; repo and `CLAUDE.md` initialized | 4 | 2–3 |
| **M1** | Problem memo (§7); each partner's `.jsonl` transcripts to date copied out | 5 | 3–4 |
| **M2** | Design document (§8); both sensors electrically alive; transcripts copied out | 7 | 8–10 |
| **M3** | Checkpoint demo: both sensors flowing through the real pipeline into real storage; at least one menu mechanism working; transcripts copied out | 10 | 25–30 |
| **M4** | Feature freeze; 48-hour soak begins; transcripts copied out | 14 | 30–40 |
| **M5** | Final submission: system, soak logs, evaluation report, process artifacts, complete transcripts | 15 | 10–14 |
| **M6** | Demo day: live demonstration, fault injection, individual defenses | 15–16 | n/a |

- **Transcript submission is not a one-time, end-of-semester task.** At every milestone from M1
  through M5, each partner copies out their raw `.jsonl` Claude Code session files (§10) covering
  the work done since the previous milestone. Building this habit in Week 5 is the point: it costs
  a minute per milestone, and it is the only way to guarantee that the transcripts graded at M5
  actually cover the whole semester rather than whatever the local 30-day retention window
...
  Week 3 on 09-10, which is consistent). **Verify against Canvas / the course site before trusting
  any date** — in particular, Week 14 lands on Thanksgiving week (Nov 23–27), and if the
  professor doesn't count fall break, everything from M4 on shifts a week later.

| Week | Dates (Mon–Fri) | Due at end of week |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | Sep 7–11 | (project announced Thu Sep 10) |
| 4 | Sep 14–18 | **M0** team formed, hardware ordered, repo + `CLAUDE.md` |
| 5 | Sep 21–25 | **M1** problem memo + transcripts |
| 7 | Oct 5–9 | **M2** design doc, both sensors electrically alive |

# CS 370 — Operating Systems — Secondary Brain

This file is auto-loaded every session in this project. It is the master index and
evolving instruction set for acting as Nick's OS-knowledge partner this semester.
I update it every time new material is processed — that's the evolution mechanism.

## Workspace layout (do not rename)

- `Lectures Slides/` — raw PDFs Nick uploads (lecture slides, handouts). Source
  material only, never edited.
- `course-notes/` — one markdown file per lecture, written by Claude after reading
  the PDF. Filename pattern: `course-notes/lecXX-topic-slug.md`
  (e.g. `course-notes/lec01-intro-to-os.md`).
- `Homeworks/` — one folder per assignment, named `hw1`, `hw2`, `hw3`, etc. Each
  `hwN/` contains the instructions Nick drops in (PDF/doc/whatever) plus any work
  product Claude helps produce. Nick creates new `hwN` folders as assignments show up.
- `Term Project/` — the semester project (Nick's folder name, top level — not under
  `Homeworks/`). Holds the original spec PDF, its full markdown conversion
  `term-project-spec.md`, and the idea brainstorm — the thinking/notes side.
  - `Term Project/Instructions/` — spec PDF, `term-project-spec.md`, `brainstorm.md` (Nick moved
    these here 2026-09-23).
  - `Term Project/submissions/` — built submission tarballs (not tracked in the repo).
  - `Term Project/term-project/` — **the actual git repo** (created 2026-09-23, `main` branch).
    Team deliverables live here: team `CLAUDE.md`, `README.md`, `PROBLEM.md`, `Makefile`,
    `src/`, `tests/`, `tools/`, and `transcripts/<partner>/<date>-<milestone>/*.jsonl`.
    Name is a placeholder — rename when the idea is locked. **Work in this directory from now
    on** so Claude Code transcripts are scoped to the project instead of mingled with HW1.
- `Quizzes/` — graded quiz photos/screenshots Nick uploads, one folder per quiz
  (`Quiz 1`…`Quiz 5`). Each folder also holds `Quiz N - Questions and Answers.pdf`
  (questions, correct answers, Nick's answers, why). Midterm 1 study material — see **Quiz Log**.
- `Midterm Prep/` — `CS 370 Midterm 1 Study Guide.pdf` (written 2026-10-07: lectures 1–11 + all quiz traps, organized by the
  exam's three sections). Practice questions for the midterm are done in chat, quiz-style, starting with Synchronization.
- `CLAUDE.md` (this file) — index of what's covered + standing instructions. The
  single source of truth for "what does this agent currently know."

## How I evolve over the semester

This is not a static prompt — it's meant to compound as the course progresses:

1. **Every lecture processed updates my working knowledge.** After reading a new
   PDF, I don't just file away a summary — I update **Current Knowledge State**
   below so future answers (including on homework) are grounded in exactly what's
   been taught, using this course's specific terminology and sequencing, not a
   generic OS textbook's.
2. **Later lectures can revise earlier understanding.** If a new lecture refines,
   corrects, or complicates a simplified first-pass model from an earlier one
   (e.g. "we said X, but actually X only holds under condition Y"), I note that
   in the earlier `course-notes/lecXX-*.md` file directly rather than silently
   carrying two inconsistent mental models.
3. **Standing behavior rules accumulate here.** If Nick corrects how I should
   explain something, what depth of detail he wants, or a professor-specific
   quirk (e.g. "this professor tests edge cases hard" or "she uses her own name
   for X"), I add it to **Standing Behavior** below so it persists automatically —
   he shouldn't have to repeat himself lecture after lecture.
4. **Homework patterns feed back too.** If a homework style, grading rubric
   quirk, or recurring assignment structure becomes clear, I log it under
   **Homework Patterns** so I calibrate help correctly on the next `hwN`.
5. **This file stays the entry point.** Any session, cold-started, should be able
   to read this file and know exactly where the course currently stands.

## Workflow: processing a new lecture PDF

When Nick drops a PDF into `Lectures Slides/` (or points to one anywhere):
1. Read the PDF in full.
2. Write `course-notes/lecXX-topic-slug.md` with:
   - **Topic & date** (if shown on the slides)
   - **Key concepts** — definitions and terminology, building on Nick's existing
     vocabulary; if a term was introduced in an earlier lecture, reference it
     (e.g. "see lec02") instead of redefining it from scratch.
   - **Mechanisms / algorithms** — how things actually work step by step,
     especially anything with a diagram, state machine, or algorithm (scheduling,
     paging, deadlock handling, etc.)
   - **Instructor's emphasis** — anything flagged as important, exam-relevant, or
     a common gotcha.
   - **Open questions / gaps** — things the slides gloss over that are worth
     asking about or watching for in later lectures.
3. Append a row to the **Lecture Log** table below.
4. Update **Current Knowledge State** below.

## Workflow: processing a new homework assignment

When Nick creates `Homeworks/hwN/` with instructions inside:
1. Read the instructions in full.
2. Cross-reference **Current Knowledge State** — flag anything the assignment

3. Default to teaching/debugging-partner mode: explain concepts, point at the
   relevant `course-notes` file, ask leading questions — don't hand over a
   finished solution unless Nick says otherwise for that assignment.
4. Log the assignment in **Homework Log** below.

## Current Knowledge State

- **OS history:** generational view (vacuum tubes → transistors/batch → ICs/multiprogramming → PCs), why OSes live long (evolve in families rather than get rewritten), rough kernel codebase scale.
- **Hardware/memory hierarchy:** von Neumann architecture; registers & special registers (PC, SP, PSW); cache lines and hit/miss mechanics; the 4-level hierarchy table (registers/cache/main memory/disk) with size, access time, managed-by, backed-by; disk capacity history; the human-scaled latency comparison (why the CPU/disk speed gap matters to OS design); the "technology drives relative-performance cycles" theme (caches, assembly usage, etc. can become obsolete and un-obsolete as hardware ratios shift).
- **Kernel abstraction:** kernel vs. user mode as a 1-bit hardware distinction; the 3 minimum hardware requirements for isolation (privileged instructions, memory protection, timer interrupts); privileged instructions; memory-protection rationale (security *and* privacy); hardware timers and why the kernel can't detect infinite loops directly; mode transitions and their 3 triggers (interrupts = async, exceptions & system calls = sync/"trap"); system call mechanics and the "assume malicious parameters" defensive-programming principle; the interrupt vector table (x86: entries 0-31 exceptions, 32-255 interrupts, entry 64 = syscall handler); the 4 kernel-to-user transition triggers (new process, resume, switch, upcall).
- **Processes:** definition (execution of a program with restricted rights); multiprogramming vs. pseudoparallelism; process vs. program distinction; how a program becomes a process (executable image → kernel copies into memory → stack/heap set aside → needs a process ID); process memory layout (text/data/heap/stack); light intro to paging (pages, non-contiguous physical mapping — full mechanics not yet covered); process state transition diagram (new/ready/running/waiting/terminated); Process Control Block (PCB) contents and purpose; context switches and what makes them slow.
- **Process creation & lifecycle:** parent/child relationships, process trees, unique PIDs; `fork()` mechanics (copies parent's memory image, return value 0 in child vs. child-PID in parent, both processes resume right after the call); classic loop patterns (chain/fan/tree) from varying which process breaks out of a fork loop; `exec()` (destroys+replaces memory image, why fork-then-exec enables fd redirection); `wait()`/`waitpid()` and the 4 pid-sign meanings; Windows' `CreateProcess` (single-step creation+load, no fork/exec split, no real process hierarchy); process groups (pgid, group leader, signal delivery only within a group); termination types (voluntary: normal/error exit; involuntary: fatal error/killed); zombies and adoption by `init`.
- **Buffer overflows & security:** stack layout mechanics (local vars, saved frame pointer, return address; stack grows high→low); how an overflow can corrupt adjacent stack variables and the return address; the 1988 Morris Worm as a worked case study (trust-based spread via `rsh`/`sendmail` + a real buffer-overflow exploit in the `finger` daemon).
- **Shells, POSIX & IPC:** shell mechanics (fork-exec-wait loop, background processes with `&`, daemons); POSIX history and purpose (System V vs. BSD incompatibility → POSIX.1 1988 → Spec 1170 1994 → Austin Group 1998 → Single UNIX Spec v3 / IEEE 1003.1-2001 approved 2001-2002); independent vs. cooperating processes and why cooperation is useful; the two IPC mechanisms — shared memory (fast, no built-in synchronization) vs. message passing (kernel-mediated, slower, simpler); producer-consumer problem and the circular buffer (in/out indices, empty = `in==out`, full = `(in+1)%SIZE==out`, N-slot buffer holds N−1 usable elements); POSIX shared-memory API (`shmget`→`shmat`→use→`shmdt`/`shmctl`); message passing's three design axes (direct/indirect communication, blocking/non-blocking synchronization, zero/bounded/unbounded buffering); Windows XP LPC as a worked example of shared memory + message passing combined in one real system.
- **Pipes:** ordinary pipes (UNIX `pipe()`/`fd[0]`/`fd[1]`, inherited via `fork()`, close-unused-end idiom for EOF semantics; Windows anonymous pipes, not auto-inherited, unidirectional) vs. named pipes/FIFOs (no parent-child relationship needed, outlive the processes using them, `mkfifo()` on UNIX, full-duplex on Windows).
- **Kernel architecture:** monolithic kernels (tight module interdependency, used by Windows/macOS/Linux, portability challenges across ISAs and especially device drivers, the 60%-device-code/90%-driver-crash Linux statistic) vs. microkernels (minimal kernel, services as user-level processes communicating only via the microkernel, mechanism-vs-policy split, isolation-is-not-free performance cost, the Windows NT→XP monolithic drift as a real case study) vs. hybrid designs.
- **Client-server communication:** RPC (request/reply model, blocking calls, RPC daemon on a port, network failure modes — size limits/reordering/loss — and the XDR fix for big-endian/little-endian data representation, client/server stub architecture); distributed objects (RPC + inheritance, CORBA/RMI, IDL, ORB, GIOP/IIOP).
- **Threads:** why threads exist (shared address space vs. process isolation, 10-100x cheaper to create than processes, GUI responsiveness is a perceived-not-actual speedup); the process model split into resource-grouping vs. execution; per-process vs. per-thread resources (address space/heap/globals/files shared; PC/registers/stack/state unique per thread); no memory protection between threads (impossible + unnecessary, since one user owns all threads in a process); the 4 benefits of multithreading (responsiveness, resource sharing, economy, scalability); concurrency (single-core interleaving) vs. parallelism (multi-core simultaneity); user-level threads (thread table in user space, invisible to kernel, "jacket" functions managing blocking calls) vs. kernel-level threads (kernel-visible, more expensive, system-wide scheduling); the three thread models — many-to-one (no true concurrency, one blocking call blocks everything), one-to-one (true concurrency, per-thread kernel overhead, the dominant real-world model), many-to-many/two-level (tunable multiplexing); thread libraries (pthreads — `pthread_create`/`join`/`exit`/`cancel`/`detach`, returns non-zero error codes and does NOT set `errno` unlike `fork()`; Java threads — `Runnable`/`Thread`/`Executor`, `.start()`/`.join()`/`.interrupt()`; Win32 threads).
- **Synchronization (lec08–lec10):** race condition = outcome depends on the order of accesses (e.g. `counter++`/`counter--` are 3 machine steps each, so final value can be 4 or 6 instead of 5); critical section = code touching shared data, structure entry/critical/exit/remainder, a process may have several; **3 requirements** — mutual exclusion, progress (only non-remainder processes decide who enters, no indefinite postponement), bounded waiting; preemptive vs. nonpreemptive kernels; **Peterson's** (exactly 2 processes, `flag[2]` + `turn`, entry `flag[i]=TRUE; turn=j; while(flag[j]&&turn==j);`, no guarantees on modern hardware); hardware assists (disable interrupts, atomic `Swap`, `TestAndSet`, x86 `XCHG`) and the N-process TestAndSet with `waiting[]` that gets bounded wait in n−1 turns; **semaphores** (atomic `wait`/`signal`, binary = mutex, counting = N resources, busy-wait spinlock vs. blocking with wait queue + `wakeup`, negative value = number waiting), deadlock from opposite lock order, priority inversion + priority inheritance; classic problems — bounded buffer (`mutex=1, empty=n, full=0`), readers-writers (first problem: writers may starve; second: readers may starve; `readcount`/`mutex`/`wrt`), dining philosophers (simple semaphore solution deadlocks if all grab the same side); how semaphores get misused (swap order, wait-wait, omissions); **monitors** (ADT with automatic mutual exclusion, one process active, entry queue) and **condition variables** (`wait`/`signal`; signal with no waiter is lost, unlike a semaphore's persistent count; signal-and-wait vs. signal-and-continue), dining philosophers via monitor (`THINKING/HUNGRY/EATING`, `test()`), starvation still possible.
- **Atomic transactions (lec11):** all-or-nothing logical unit of work, commit vs. abort, rollback; write-ahead log (record = transaction, item, old value, new value; log written *before* data); undo/redo are idempotent; recovery rule (start without commit = undo, start + commit = redo); checkpoints shorten recovery (commit before checkpoint = no redo); conflict (same item + at least one write), conflict serializability, shared/exclusive locks, two-phase locking (growing/shrinking, deadlock possible), timestamp protocols (no deadlock, R/W-timestamps, reject + roll back on "from the future" accesses); Solaris adaptive mutex/turnstiles, Linux `preempt_count`/`atomic_t`/mutex.
- **CPU scheduling (lec12, NOT on midterm 1):** CPU-I/O burst cycle (I/O-bound = many short bursts, CPU-bound = few long), preemptive vs. nonpreemptive (needs timer), dispatcher + dispatch latency, criteria (utilization, throughput, turnaround, waiting, response), FCFS (convoy effect), SJF (optimal average wait only when all jobs arrive together), SRTF (starvation, pessimal variance), EWMA burst prediction `τ(n+1)=α·t(n)+(1−α)τ(n)`.
- **Not yet covered:** scheduling algorithms beyond FCFS/SJF (priority, round-robin, multilevel feedback queues, lottery, Linux CFS — previewed only), full virtual memory/paging details, file systems, I/O subsystems, deadlock as its own topic (only seen as examples inside synchronization), sockets/networking mechanics. Don't reach for these until they show up in a lecture.

**DECIDED — Dark Sky Monitor (locked 2026-09-23).** An offline Pi device that measures sky
brightness and cloud cover at one site and grades the night **GOOD / MARGINAL / POOR / UNKNOWN**
with the evidence behind the verdict and a confidence score. Chosen after ~110 candidate ideas
across 12 brainstorm rounds in
[brainstorm.md](Term%20Project/Instructions/brainstorm.md) (kept for the record; the filters Nick

**Full engineering design review:** `Term Project/term-project/docs/design-review.md` (20 sections).
Read it before answering any design question. Nine places Nick's original framing had to change are
recorded there, the load-bearing ones being:
- **Three sensors, not two** — humidity confounds the IR cloud signal, because water vapour radiates
  in the IR window, so a humid *clear* sky mimics overcast without a humidity correction.
- **The core fusion insight (this is the memo's best paragraph):** a brightness sensor alone is not

## Current Knowledge State

- **OS history:** generational view (vacuum tubes → transistors/batch → ICs/multiprogramming → PCs), why OSes live long (evolve in families rather than get rewritten), rough kernel codebase scale.

- **Buffer overflows & security:** stack layout mechanics (local vars, saved frame pointer, return address; stack grows high→low); how an overflow can corrupt adjacent stack variables and the return address; the 1988 Morris Worm as a worked case study (trust-based spread via `rsh`/`sendmail` + a real buffer-overflow exploit in the `finger` daemon).
- **Shells, POSIX & IPC:** shell mechanics (fork-exec-wait loop, background processes with `&`, daemons); POSIX history and purpose (System V vs. BSD incompatibility → POSIX.1 1988 → Spec 1170 1994 → Austin Group 1998 → Single UNIX Spec v3 / IEEE 1003.1-2001 approved 2001-2002); independent vs. cooperating processes and why cooperation is useful; the two IPC mechanisms — shared memory (fast, no built-in synchronization) vs. message passing (kernel-mediated, slower, simpler); producer-consumer problem and the circular buffer (in/out indices, empty = `in==out`, full = `(in+1)%SIZE==out`, N-slot buffer holds N−1 usable elements); POSIX shared-memory API (`shmget`→`shmat`→use→`shmdt`/`shmctl`); message passing's three design axes (direct/indirect communication, blocking/non-blocking synchronization, zero/bounded/unbounded buffering); Windows XP LPC as a worked example of shared memory + message passing combined in one real system.
- **Pipes:** ordinary pipes (UNIX `pipe()`/`fd[0]`/`fd[1]`, inherited via `fork()`, close-unused-end idiom for EOF semantics; Windows anonymous pipes, not auto-inherited, unidirectional) vs. named pipes/FIFOs (no parent-child relationship needed, outlive the processes using them, `mkfifo()` on UNIX, full-duplex on Windows).
- **Kernel architecture:** monolithic kernels (tight module interdependency, used by Windows/macOS/Linux, portability challenges across ISAs and especially device drivers, the 60%-device-code/90%-driver-crash Linux statistic) vs. microkernels (minimal kernel, services as user-level processes communicating only via the microkernel, mechanism-vs-policy split, isolation-is-not-free performance cost, the Windows NT→XP monolithic drift as a real case study) vs. hybrid designs.
- **Client-server communication:** RPC (request/reply model, blocking calls, RPC daemon on a port, network failure modes — size limits/reordering/loss — and the XDR fix for big-endian/little-endian data representation, client/server stub architecture); distributed objects (RPC + inheritance, CORBA/RMI, IDL, ORB, GIOP/IIOP).
- **Threads:** why threads exist (shared address space vs. process isolation, 10-100x cheaper to create than processes, GUI responsiveness is a perceived-not-actual speedup); the process model split into resource-grouping vs. execution; per-process vs. per-thread resources (address space/heap/globals/files shared; PC/registers/stack/state unique per thread); no memory protection between threads (impossible + unnecessary, since one user owns all threads in a process); the 4 benefits of multithreading (responsiveness, resource sharing, economy, scalability); concurrency (single-core interleaving) vs. parallelism (multi-core simultaneity); user-level threads (thread table in user space, invisible to kernel, "jacket" functions managing blocking calls) vs. kernel-level threads (kernel-visible, more expensive, system-wide scheduling); the three thread models — many-to-one (no true concurrency, one blocking call blocks everything), one-to-one (true concurrency, per-thread kernel overhead, the dominant real-world model), many-to-many/two-level (tunable multiplexing); thread libraries (pthreads — `pthread_create`/`join`/`exit`/`cancel`/`detach`, returns non-zero error codes and does NOT set `errno` unlike `fork()`; Java threads — `Runnable`/`Thread`/`Executor`, `.start()`/`.join()`/`.interrupt()`; Win32 threads).
- **Synchronization (lec08–lec10):** race condition = outcome depends on the order of accesses (e.g. `counter++`/`counter--` are 3 machine steps each, so final value can be 4 or 6 instead of 5); critical section = code touching shared data, structure entry/critical/exit/remainder, a process may have several; **3 requirements** — mutual exclusion, progress (only non-remainder processes decide who enters, no indefinite postponement), bounded waiting; preemptive vs. nonpreemptive kernels; **Peterson's** (exactly 2 processes, `flag[2]` + `turn`, entry `flag[i]=TRUE; turn=j; while(flag[j]&&turn==j);`, no guarantees on modern hardware); hardware assists (disable interrupts, atomic `Swap`, `TestAndSet`, x86 `XCHG`) and the N-process TestAndSet with `waiting[]` that gets bounded wait in n−1 turns; **semaphores** (atomic `wait`/`signal`, binary = mutex, counting = N resources, busy-wait spinlock vs. blocking with wait queue + `wakeup`, negative value = number waiting), deadlock from opposite lock order, priority inversion + priority inheritance; classic problems — bounded buffer (`mutex=1, empty=n, full=0`), readers-writers (first problem: writers may starve; second: readers may starve; `readcount`/`mutex`/`wrt`), dining philosophers (simple semaphore solution deadlocks if all grab the same side); how semaphores get misused (swap order, wait-wait, omissions); **monitors** (ADT with automatic mutual exclusion, one process active, entry queue) and **condition variables** (`wait`/`signal`; signal with no waiter is lost, unlike a semaphore's persistent count; signal-and-wait vs. signal-and-continue), dining philosophers via monitor (`THINKING/HUNGRY/EATING`, `test()`), starvation still possible.
- **Atomic transactions (lec11):** all-or-nothing logical unit of work, commit vs. abort, rollback; write-ahead log (record = transaction, item, old value, new value; log written *before* data); undo/redo are idempotent; recovery rule (start without commit = undo, start + commit = redo); checkpoints shorten recovery (commit before checkpoint = no redo); conflict (same item + at least one write), conflict serializability, shared/exclusive locks, two-phase locking (growing/shrinking, deadlock possible), timestamp protocols (no deadlock, R/W-timestamps, reject + roll back on "from the future" accesses); Solaris adaptive mutex/turnstiles, Linux `preempt_count`/`atomic_t`/mutex.
- **CPU scheduling (lec12, NOT on midterm 1):** CPU-I/O burst cycle (I/O-bound = many short bursts, CPU-bound = few long), preemptive vs. nonpreemptive (needs timer), dispatcher + dispatch latency, criteria (utilization, throughput, turnaround, waiting, response), FCFS (convoy effect), SJF (optimal average wait only when all jobs arrive together), SRTF (starvation, pessimal variance), EWMA burst prediction `τ(n+1)=α·t(n)+(1−α)τ(n)`.
- **Not yet covered:** scheduling algorithms beyond FCFS/SJF (priority, round-robin, multilevel feedback queues, lottery, Linux CFS — previewed only), full virtual memory/paging details, file systems, I/O subsystems, deadlock as its own topic (only seen as examples inside synchronization), sockets/networking mechanics. Don't reach for these until they show up in a lecture.

## Current Knowledge State

- **OS history:** generational view (vacuum tubes → transistors/batch → ICs/multiprogramming → PCs), why OSes live long (evolve in families rather than get rewritten), rough kernel codebase scale.
- **Hardware/memory hierarchy:** von Neumann architecture; registers & special registers (PC, SP, PSW); cache lines and hit/miss mechanics; the 4-level hierarchy table (registers/cache/main memory/disk) with size, access time, managed-by, backed-by; disk capacity history; the human-scaled latency comparison (why the CPU/disk speed gap matters to OS design); the "technology drives relative-performance cycles" theme (caches, assembly usage, etc. can become obsolete and un-obsolete as hardware ratios shift).
- **Kernel abstraction:** kernel vs. user mode as a 1-bit hardware distinction; the 3 minimum hardware requirements for isolation (privileged instructions, memory protection, timer interrupts); privileged instructions; memory-protection rationale (security *and* privacy); hardware timers and why the kernel can't detect infinite loops directly; mode transitions and their 3 triggers (interrupts = async, exceptions & system calls = sync/"trap"); system call mechanics and the "assume malicious parameters" defensive-programming principle; the interrupt vector table (x86: entries 0-31 exceptions, 32-255 interrupts, entry 64 = syscall handler); the 4 kernel-to-user transition triggers (new process, resume, switch, upcall).
- **Processes:** definition (execution of a program with restricted rights); multiprogramming vs. pseudoparallelism; process vs. program distinction; how a program becomes a process (executable image → kernel copies into memory → stack/heap set aside → needs a process ID); process memory layout (text/data/heap/stack); light intro to paging (pages, non-contiguous physical mapping — full mechanics not yet covered); process state transition diagram (new/ready/running/waiting/terminated); Process Control Block (PCB) contents and purpose; context switches and what makes them slow.
- **Process creation & lifecycle:** parent/child relationships, process trees, unique PIDs; `fork()` mechanics (copies parent's memory image, return value 0 in child vs. child-PID in parent, both processes resume right after the call); classic loop patterns (chain/fan/tree) from varying which process breaks out of a fork loop; `exec()` (destroys+replaces memory image, why fork-then-exec enables fd redirection); `wait()`/`waitpid()` and the 4 pid-sign meanings; Windows' `CreateProcess` (single-step creation+load, no fork/exec split, no real process hierarchy); process groups (pgid, group leader, signal delivery only within a group); termination types (voluntary: normal/error exit; involuntary: fatal error/killed); zombies and adoption by `init`.
- **Buffer overflows & security:** stack layout mechanics (local vars, saved frame pointer, return address; stack grows high→low); how an overflow can corrupt adjacent stack variables and the return address; the 1988 Morris Worm as a worked case study (trust-based spread via `rsh`/`sendmail` + a real buffer-overflow exploit in the `finger` daemon).
- **Shells, POSIX & IPC:** shell mechanics (fork-exec-wait loop, background processes with `&`, daemons); POSIX history and purpose (System V vs. BSD incompatibility → POSIX.1 1988 → Spec 1170 1994 → Austin Group 1998 → Single UNIX Spec v3 / IEEE 1003.1-2001 approved 2001-2002); independent vs. cooperating processes and why cooperation is useful; the two IPC mechanisms — shared memory (fast, no built-in synchronization) vs. message passing (kernel-mediated, slower, simpler); producer-consumer problem and the circular buffer (in/out indices, empty = `in==out`, full = `(in+1)%SIZE==out`, N-slot buffer holds N−1 usable elements); POSIX shared-memory API (`shmget`→`shmat`→use→`shmdt`/`shmctl`); message passing's three design axes (direct/indirect communication, blocking/non-blocking synchronization, zero/bounded/unbounded buffering); Windows XP LPC as a worked example of shared memory + message passing combined in one real system.
- **Pipes:** ordinary pipes (UNIX `pipe()`/`fd[0]`/`fd[1]`, inherited via `fork()`, close-unused-end idiom for EOF semantics; Windows anonymous pipes, not auto-inherited, unidirectional) vs. named pipes/FIFOs (no parent-child relationship needed, outlive the processes using them, `mkfifo()` on UNIX, full-duplex on Windows).
- **Kernel architecture:** monolithic kernels (tight module interdependency, used by Windows/macOS/Linux, portability challenges across ISAs and especially device drivers, the 60%-device-code/90%-driver-crash Linux statistic) vs. microkernels (minimal kernel, services as user-level processes communicating only via the microkernel, mechanism-vs-policy split, isolation-is-not-free performance cost, the Windows NT→XP monolithic drift as a real case study) vs. hybrid designs.
- **Client-server communication:** RPC (request/reply model, blocking calls, RPC daemon on a port, network failure modes — size limits/reordering/loss — and the XDR fix for big-endian/little-endian data representation, client/server stub architecture); distributed objects (RPC + inheritance, CORBA/RMI, IDL, ORB, GIOP/IIOP).
- **Threads:** why threads exist (shared address space vs. process isolation, 10-100x cheaper to create than processes, GUI responsiveness is a perceived-not-actual speedup); the process model split into resource-grouping vs. execution; per-process vs. per-thread resources (address space/heap/globals/files shared; PC/registers/stack/state unique per thread); no memory protection between threads (impossible + unnecessary, since one user owns all threads in a process); the 4 benefits of multithreading (responsiveness, resource sharing, economy, scalability); concurrency (single-core interleaving) vs. parallelism (multi-core simultaneity); user-level threads (thread table in user space, invisible to kernel, "jacket" functions managing blocking calls) vs. kernel-level threads (kernel-visible, more expensive, system-wide scheduling); the three thread models — many-to-one (no true concurrency, one blocking call blocks everything), one-to-one (true concurrency, per-thread kernel overhead, the dominant real-world model), many-to-many/two-level (tunable multiplexing); thread libraries (pthreads — `pthread_create`/`join`/`exit`/`cancel`/`detach`, returns non-zero error codes and does NOT set `errno` unlike `fork()`; Java threads — `Runnable`/`Thread`/`Executor`, `.start()`/`.join()`/`.interrupt()`; Win32 threads).
- **Synchronization (lec08–lec10):** race condition = outcome depends on the order of accesses (e.g. `counter++`/`counter--` are 3 machine steps each, so final value can be 4 or 6 instead of 5); critical section = code touching shared data, structure entry/critical/exit/remainder, a process may have several; **3 requirements** — mutual exclusion, progress (only non-remainder processes decide who enters, no indefinite postponement), bounded waiting; preemptive vs. nonpreemptive kernels; **Peterson's** (exactly 2 processes, `flag[2]` + `turn`, entry `flag[i]=TRUE; turn=j; while(flag[j]&&turn==j);`, no guarantees on modern hardware); hardware assists (disable interrupts, atomic `Swap`, `TestAndSet`, x86 `XCHG`) and the N-process TestAndSet with `waiting[]` that gets bounded wait in n−1 turns; **semaphores** (atomic `wait`/`signal`, binary = mutex, counting = N resources, busy-wait spinlock vs. blocking with wait queue + `wakeup`, negative value = number waiting), deadlock from opposite lock order, priority inversion + priority inheritance; classic problems — bounded buffer (`mutex=1, empty=n, full=0`), readers-writers (first problem: writers may starve; second: readers may starve; `readcount`/`mutex`/`wrt`), dining philosophers (simple semaphore solution deadlocks if all grab the same side); how semaphores get misused (swap order, wait-wait, omissions); **monitors** (ADT with automatic mutual exclusion, one process active, entry queue) and **condition variables** (`wait`/`signal`; signal with no waiter is lost, unlike a semaphore's persistent count; signal-and-wait vs. signal-and-continue), dining philosophers via monitor (`THINKING/HUNGRY/EATING`, `test()`), starvation still possible.
- **Atomic transactions (lec11):** all-or-nothing logical unit of work, commit vs. abort, rollback; write-ahead log (record = transaction, item, old value, new value; log written *before* data); undo/redo are idempotent; recovery rule (start without commit = undo, start + commit = redo); checkpoints shorten recovery (commit before checkpoint = no redo); conflict (same item + at least one write), conflict serializability, shared/exclusive locks, two-phase locking (growing/shrinking, deadlock possible), timestamp protocols (no deadlock, R/W-timestamps, reject + roll back on "from the future" accesses); Solaris adaptive mutex/turnstiles, Linux `preempt_count`/`atomic_t`/mutex.
- **CPU scheduling (lec12, NOT on midterm 1):** CPU-I/O burst cycle (I/O-bound = many short bursts, CPU-bound = few long), preemptive vs. nonpreemptive (needs timer), dispatcher + dispatch latency, criteria (utilization, throughput, turnaround, waiting, response), FCFS (convoy effect), SJF (optimal average wait only when all jobs arrive together), SRTF (starvation, pessimal variance), EWMA burst prediction `τ(n+1)=α·t(n)+(1−α)τ(n)`.
- **Not yet covered:** scheduling algorithms beyond FCFS/SJF (priority, round-robin, multilevel feedback queues, lottery, Linux CFS — previewed only), full virtual memory/paging details, file systems, I/O subsystems, deadlock as its own topic (only seen as examples inside synchronization), sockets/networking mechanics. # Design Document (M2)

> **M2, 2026-10-27: drafted by Liam (Nick unavailable); the decisions in Nick's area were confirmed by Nick on 2026-10-28.**
> **(a)** = **assumed (datasheet), not yet measured.** The sensors are wired and identified (2026-10-28,
> hardware-log §1–2), but no performance number here is measured yet.

## Architecture

Seven single-threaded (`1T`) processes; *rec* = one sealed 48-byte record; sample periods 5/1/10 s.

```
  TSL2591 @0x29 (a)          MLX90614 @0x5A (a)          BME280 @0x76 (a)
        └───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┘
                                    │ I2C bus 1, 3.3 V, 100 kHz (a): ≈2.6 transfers/s in total
════════════════════════════════════╪════════ kernel: i2c-bcm2835 + i2c-dev, /dev/i2c-1 (a) ══
        ┌───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┐
        │ 0.4 xfer/s (a)            │ 2 xfer/s (a)               │ 0.2 xfer/s (a)    ioctl(I2C_RDWR)
════════╪═══════════════════════════╪════════════════════════════╪════════════════════ user
   ┌────▼─────┐                ┌────▼─────┐                 ┌────▼─────┐
   │ skyd  1T │                │cloudd 1T │                 │ envd  1T │
   └────┬─────┘                └────┬─────┘                 └────┬─────┘
        │ 0.2 rec/s → ring 1        │ 1 rec/s → ring 2           │ 0.1 rec/s → ring 3
        └───────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┘   shm, 1024 × 48 B each
                                    │ 1.3 rec/s read · 1.3 sem_post/s
                            ┌───────▼────────┐   AF_UNIX stream    ┌────────────┐
                            │  fusiond   1T  │◄───── on demand ───►│  dsq (CLI) │◄── user, over SSH
                            └───────┬────────┘                     └─────┬──────┘
                                    │ AF_UNIX SEQPACKET 1.37 rec/s       │ read-only, on demand
                            ┌───────▼────────┐                           │
              dskyd ───────►│  stored    1T  │                           │
          SEQPACKET 6 rec/h └───────┬────────┘                           │
                                    │ write() every 10 s (≈660 B) · fsync() every 60 s
════════════════════════════════════╪════════════════════════════════════╪════════════ kernel
                     page cache → ext4 → mmc driver → 16 GB microSD: ≈5.7 MB/day
```

Every channel is `AF_UNIX`, a pipe, shm or a signal: **no IP sockets**. **Supervision:** `dskyd`
(under systemd) fork/execs the five children, watches a per-child liveness pipe (EOF = died, 20 s
silent = hung → `SIGKILL`), restarts with 1→60 s backoff, parks an absent sensor as `DEAD` with a
60 s re-probe, and logs hourly HEARTBEATs; stderr → journald. Rates and channel details:
[`docs/record-and-ipc.md`](docs/record-and-ipc.md).

## Mechanism mapping

Each GOOD acted on costs the user **30–45 min of setup or a 30–60 min drive**; the product's value
is a **site baseline built over weeks** (PROBLEM.md).

**E: multi-process + IPC + supervisor** (`dskyd`, one process per sensor, `fusiond`; shm rings,
`AF_UNIX` sockets). **R-E1:** a dead, hung or unplugged sensor turns the verdict UNKNOWN within
**60 s** while the others keep sampling. **R-E2:** a crash costs ≤ **10 s** of that sensor's
data. *Why:* at a dark site, overcast reads *darker* than clear, so a silent IR sensor yields a
confident false GOOD, the error that wastes the evening. In one process, one hung `ioctl` stalls
every sensor; separate processes keep failures local, `fusiond` flags staleness after 3 missed
periods (≤ 30 s), and analysis restarts without stopping sampling.

**D: crash-consistent storage** (`stored`, record format). **R-D1:** a power cut loses
≤ **60 s** of records, never an earlier one. **R-D2:** automatic recovery, **20/20** pulled-plug
tests. **R-D3:** ≥ **180 days** raw plus all rollups fit the 16 GB card. *Why:* the baseline *is*
the product's memory, and a yard extension cord sees brownouts (spec §17). Verdicts use 30-min
windows, so losing ≤ 60 s (≤ 3 %) can't flip a night: hence `fsync` every 60 s, with 10 s write
batching to spare the card; CRC-sealed fixed-size records make truncation a complete recovery.

**Ring invariants (E)** ([full](docs/record-and-ipc.md)): chosen for **decoupled lifetimes, not
speed**. Publish-after-write (release/acquire on `head`), CRC check on read, never overwrite
unread (`head − tail < N`), reader-restart duplicates removed by (source, run, seq), lock-free
`_Static_assert` (**assumed, confirmed at build on the Pi**). **Rejected:** C, F (nothing at 1.3
rec/s has a deadline or rate to sustain); A is a stretch; B needs a pulse-output sensor.

## Failure-mode table

Each row names its injection (spec §9). Log lines, shown from LEVEL on, are the **planned format
(`<ISO time> <mono s> <proc>[pid] LEVEL event k=v`), not captured output**.

| Component | Failure (injected by) | Detected by → system does | Log shows |
|----------|----------------|--------------------------------------------|------------------------|
| sensor daemon | unplugged (pull jumper) | 3 failed reads, errno `EREMOTEIO`/`ENXIO` (a) → FAULT, exit "absent"; `dskyd`: `DEAD`, re-probe 60 s; UNKNOWN | `ERROR cloudd read_fail errno=EREMOTEIO n=3` |
| sensor daemon | hung (`kill -STOP`) | 20 s without a liveness byte → `SIGKILL`, restart | `WARN dskyd envd hung action=SIGKILL` |
| any child | crash (`kill -9`) | pipe EOF + `SIGCHLD` → restart, backoff 1→60 s, new run; rings hold ≥17 min for `fusiond`; `fusiond` buffers 4096 recs for `stored` | `WARN dskyd skyd died sig=9 run=4` |
| any child | storm (5× `kill -9` in 5 min) | → `DEAD`, re-probe 60 s; the rest keeps running | `ERROR dskyd cloudd storm state=DEAD` |
| I2C bus | all lost (pull head's 3.3 V) | all absent ≤ 30 s → UNKNOWN "no sensors"; a real lockup can't be injected safely and takes this path | `ERROR dskyd all_sensors_absent` |
| reading | saturated (flashlight) | TSL2591 range check → SAMPLE without `VALID`, ignored by `fusiond` | `WARN skyd saturated ch0=65535` |
| IR window | dew (breathe; `SYNTHETIC`) | dew margin < 1 °C + ΔT collapse, brightness steady (a) → "likely condensation, not cloud" | `WARN fusiond condensation` |
| `stored` | power cut (pull plug) | boot CRC scan → truncate at the first bad record | `WARN stored recover cut_bytes=31` |
| `stored` | `remount,ro`; ballast to < 2 GB | write error → exit, recover on restart; `statvfs()` → raw off, rollups on | `ERROR stored write_fail errno=EROFS` |
| `dskyd` | crash (`kill -9`) | systemd → children exit (`PDEATHSIG`); tree restarts in 1 s | `dskyd.service: Main process exited` |
| clock | no RTC or network (offline reboot) | `adjtimex()` unsynced → `CLOCK_UNSYNC`, UNKNOWN; sampling continues | `WARN fusiond clock_unsync` |
| any process | slow leak (soak; not injectable) | hourly RSS in HEARTBEAT → trend | `INFO dskyd hb fusiond rss_kb=812` |
| `dsq` | query, `fusiond` down | `connect()` fails → "UNKNOWN (hub down)"; history readable; exit 2 | `state: UNKNOWN (hub down)` |

## Storage and data

Decided, not yet built, except parts marked *implemented*; details in [`docs/record-and-ipc.md`](docs/record-and-ipc.md).

- **Record** (*implemented*): 48 B, little-endian, CRC-32-sealed. Kinds: SAMPLE (raw fixed-point
  values), FEATURE/STATE, HEARTBEAT, FAULT, START. Failed read → FAULT; implausible value →
  SAMPLE without `VALID`; replayed or provoked → `SYNTHETIC`. `seq` counts per (source, run),
  each run opened by START, so a gap within a run is provable loss. **≈5.7 MB/day, ≈1.0 GB per
  180 days** (computed; checked after the first 24 h run).
- **Files, durability, retention:** `data/seg-NNNNNN.dsm` = 24 B header (*implemented*) +
  records, one per night, rotated at local noon (24 h monotonic if unsynced), ≤ 32 MB. `write()`
  every 10 s or 64 recs; `fsync()` every 60 s, at rotation and shutdown, plus the directory on
  segment creation. Raw kept 180 days, nightly rollups forever; < 2 GB free → raw writes stop.
- **Power cut mid-write:** ≤ 60 s lost. On start, `stored` CRC-checks each slot of the open
  segment (closed ones were `fsync()`ed), truncates at the first bad one (torn or zero tail; zeros
  never pass, *tested*) and logs counts; a 1–23 B file named like our segment is a torn header,
  recreated. *Implemented* (116 checks, ASan/valgrind clean): header checks, refusing foreign
  files and unsealed records, stop after a failed write. M3: recovery, batching, `fsync`.

## Constraints and substitutions

| Area | Ideal → actual | What the gap costs |
|------------|-------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| Brightness | calibrated SQM → TSL2591, no reference | **relative to the site baseline**, never absolute mag/arcsec² |
| Cloud | commercial sensor → MLX90614 + BME280, own humidity fit | if humid-clear and overcast don't separate, the claim narrows to dry nights |
| Hardware | Adafruit, 2 GB Pi, endurance card, DS3231, enclosure → clones, 1 GB Pi 4, standard 16 GB, no RTC (to be ordered), no enclosure | BME280 verified genuine (chip ID `0x60`); MLX FOV unknown; offline reboot → UNKNOWN until network time; no outdoor runs; Pi, card fine (a) |
| Kits | one → two: `darksky.local` (Nick), `starlight.local` (Liam) | soak, demo, all evaluation numbers **only from `darksky.local`**; kit differences in hardware log |
| User, truth | named astronomer, months of labels → archetype; obs. log + `SYNTHETIC` provoked data | requirements from PROBLEM.md; counts, not %, on small n |
| Budget | $50–80 per team (spec §17) → Nick ≈ $68 (Pi $35 + sensors ≈ $33), Liam $77 (Pi $45 + sensors $32): **team ≈ $145** | **≈ $65 over the guideline's top (≈ 1.8×)**, before unrecorded PSUs, SD cards, RTC, enclosure; each kit alone is within it |

**"Both sensors electrically alive": met 2026-10-28** on `darksky.local`. All three answer at
`0x29`/`0x5a`/`0x76`; BME280 ID `0x60`, TSL2591 ID `0x50`; first live readings (hardware-log §1–2).
Still to do: §3–5 (sky vs. wall, window material, dark offset); then correct the (a) values.

## Evaluation plan

Targets are commitments, not results. (a) = hardware-dependent; loaded = `stress-ng --cpu 4`.

| # | Measurement | Method | Target |
|-|----------------|------------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| 1 | Sample → hub latency | `t_mono` at read vs. ring dequeue; 24 h idle + 24 h loaded; distributions | p99 ≤ 50 ms idle, ≤ 200 ms loaded (a) |
| 2 | Sample → durable | read time vs. the covering `fsync()` | p99 ≤ 61 s, by design |
| 3 | Unplug → UNKNOWN | pull a sensor 20×; last good sample → STATE | max ≤ 60 s (R-E1) |
| 4 | CPU, RSS per process | hourly HEARTBEAT over the 48 h soak, plotted | total < 5 % of a core; RSS ≤ 8 MB each; growth ≤ 1 % after hour 1 (a) |
| 5 | **Domain:** cloud state | manual sky observation (okta) logged at the same time as the device reading; ΔT_corr class (clear / broken / overcast) vs. it; confusion matrix | ≥ 80 % agreement on ≥ 40 obs. |
| 6 | **Domain:** night verdict | GOOD/MARGINAL/POOR vs. the observer's verdict, as N of M | ≥ 70 % on ≥ 20 obs. |
| 7 | **E:** `kill -9` | 20 kills × 5 children, scripted | detect ≤ 1 s; new sample ≤ 10 s (R-E2); no loss elsewhere |
| 8 | **E:** hang | `kill -STOP` each sensor daemon 10× | `SIGKILL` at 20 ± 1 s; UNKNOWN ≤ 60 s |
| 9 | **E:** isolation cost | interval jitter, 1 vs. 3 daemons on the bus, idle and loaded | p99 ≤ 50 ms (a); > 100 ms → I2C broker |
| 10 | **D:** `fsync` sweep | 1 / 10 / 60 / 300 s; card writes (`/proc/diskstats`), `fsync()` time distribution | ≤ 30 MB/day at 60 s (a); full curve |
| 11 | **D:** power cut | pull the plug mid-write ≥ 20×, outside the soak | 20/20 automatic; ≤ 60 s lost each (R-D1, R-D2) |

| clock | no RTC or network (offline reboot) | `adjtimex()` unsynced → `CLOCK_UNSYNC`, UNKNOWN; sampling continues | `WARN fusiond clock_unsync` |
| any process | slow leak (soak; not injectable) | hourly RSS in HEARTBEAT → trend | `INFO dskyd hb fusiond rss_kb=812` |
| `dsq` | query, `fusiond` down | `connect()` fails → "UNKNOWN (hub down)"; history readable; exit 2 | `state: UNKNOWN (hub down)` |

## Storage and data

Decided, not yet built, except parts marked *implemented*; details in [`docs/record-and-ipc.md`](docs/record-and-ipc.md).

- **Record** (*implemented*): 48 B, little-endian, CRC-32-sealed. Kinds: SAMPLE (raw fixed-point
  values), FEATURE/STATE, HEARTBEAT, FAULT, START. Failed read → FAULT; implausible value →
  SAMPLE without `VALID`; replayed or provoked → `SYNTHETIC`. `seq` counts per (source, run),
  each run opened by START, so a gap within a run is provable loss. **≈5.7 MB/day, ≈1.0 GB per
  180 days** (computed; checked after the first 24 h run).
- **Files, durability, retention:** `data/seg-NNNNNN.dsm` = 24 B header (*implemented*) +
  records, one per night, rotated at local noon (24 h monotonic if unsynced), ≤ 32 MB. `write()`
  every 10 s or 64 recs; `fsync()` every 60 s, at rotation and shutdown, plus the directory on
  segment creation. Raw kept 180 days, nightly rollups forever; < 2 GB free → raw writes stop.
- **Power cut mid-write:** ≤ 60 s lost. On start, `stored` CRC-checks each slot of the open
  segment (closed ones were `fsync()`ed), truncates at the first bad one (torn or zero tail; zeros
  never pass, *tested*) and logs counts; a 1–23 B file named like our segment is a torn header,
  recreated. *Implemented* (116 checks, ASan/valgrind clean): header checks, refusing foreign
  files and unsealed records, stop after a failed write. M3: recovery, batching, `fsync`.

## Constraints and substitutions

| Area | Ideal → actual | What the gap costs |
|------------|-------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| Brightness | calibrated SQM → TSL2591, no reference | **relative to the site baseline**, never absolute mag/arcsec² |
| Cloud | commercial sensor → MLX90614 + BME280, own humidity fit | if humid-clear and overcast don't separate, the claim narrows to dry nights |
| Hardware | Adafruit, 2 GB Pi, endurance card, DS3231, enclosure → clones, 1 GB Pi 4, standard 16 GB, no RTC (to be ordered), no enclosure | BME280 verified genuine (chip ID `0x60`); MLX FOV unknown; offline reboot → UNKNOWN until network time; no outdoor runs; Pi, card fine (a) |
| Kits | one → two: `darksky.local` (Nick), `starlight.local` (Liam) | soak, demo, all evaluation numbers **only from `darksky.local`**; kit differences in hardware log |
| User, truth | named astronomer, months of labels → archetype; obs. log + `SYNTHETIC` provoked data | requirements from PROBLEM.md; counts, not %, on small n |
| Budget | $50–80 per team (spec §17) → Nick ≈ $68 (Pi $35 + sensors ≈ $33), Liam $77 (Pi $45 + sensors $32): **team ≈ $145** | **≈ $65 over the guideline's top (≈ 1.8×)**, before unrecorded PSUs, SD cards, RTC, enclosure; each kit alone is within it |

**"Both sensors electrically alive": met 2026-10-28** on `darksky.local`. All three answer at
`0x29`/`0x5a`/`0x76`; BME280 ID `0x60`, TSL2591 ID `0x50`; first live readings (hardware-log §1–2).
Still to do: §3–5 (sky vs. wall, window material, dark offset); then correct the (a) values.

## Evaluation plan

Targets are commitments, not results. (a) = hardware-dependent; loaded = `stress-ng --cpu 4`.

| # | Measurement | Method | Target |
|-|----------------|------------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| 1 | Sample → hub latency | `t_mono` at read vs. ring dequeue; 24 h idle + 24 h loaded; distributions | p99 ≤ 50 ms idle, ≤ 200 ms loaded (a) |
| 2 | Sample → durable | read time vs. the covering `fsync()` | p99 ≤ 61 s, by design |
| 3 | Unplug → UNKNOWN | pull a sensor 20×; last good sample → STATE | max ≤ 60 s (R-E1) |
| 4 | CPU, RSS per process | hourly HEARTBEAT over the 48 h soak, plotted | total < 5 % of a core; RSS ≤ 8 MB each; growth ≤ 1 % after hour 1 (a) |
| 5 | **Domain:** cloud state | manual sky observation (okta) logged at the same time as the device reading; ΔT_corr class (clear / broken / overcast) vs. it; confusion matrix | ≥ 80 % agreement on ≥ 40 obs. |
| 6 | **Domain:** night verdict | GOOD/MARGINAL/POOR vs. the observer's verdict, as N of M | ≥ 70 % on ≥ 20 obs. |
| 7 | **E:** `kill -9` | 20 kills × 5 children, scripted | detect ≤ 1 s; new sample ≤ 10 s (R-E2); no loss elsewhere |
| 8 | **E:** hang | `kill -STOP` each sensor daemon 10× | `SIGKILL` at 20 ± 1 s; UNKNOWN ≤ 60 s |
| 9 | **E:** isolation cost | interval jitter, 1 vs. 3 daemons on the bus, idle and loaded | p99 ≤ 50 ms (a); > 100 ms → I2C broker |
| 10 | **D:** `fsync` sweep | 1 / 10 / 60 / 300 s; card writes (`/proc/diskstats`), `fsync()` time distribution | ≤ 30 MB/day at 60 s (a); full curve |
| 11 | **D:** power cut | pull the plug mid-write ≥ 20×, outside the soak | 20/20 automatic; ≤ 60 s lost each (R-D1, R-D2) |

#ifndef DSM_RECORD_H
#define DSM_RECORD_H

#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stddef.h>
#include <stdint.h>

#define DSM_SCHEMA_VER 1

/* Starts at 1 so a zeroed record never looks like a real kind. */
enum dsm_kind {
    DSM_KIND_SAMPLE    = 1,
    DSM_KIND_FEATURE   = 2,
    DSM_KIND_STATE     = 3,
    DSM_KIND_HEARTBEAT = 4,
    DSM_KIND_FAULT     = 5,
};

/* Bits in dsm_record.flags. They describe the reading, not the bytes.
 * SYNTHETIC is required by the spec: replayed or made-up data has to be
 * labeled everywhere it appears, so it is part of the record itself. */
enum dsm_flag {
    DSM_FLAG_VALID       = 1u << 0,
    DSM_FLAG_STALE       = 1u << 1,
    DSM_FLAG_SYNTHETIC   = 1u << 2,
    DSM_FLAG_CALIBRATING = 1u << 3,
};

/* One record, exactly as it sits on disk. */
struct dsm_record {
    uint64_t t_mono_ns;   /* CLOCK_MONOTONIC: for measuring intervals */
    uint64_t t_real_ns;   /* CLOCK_REALTIME: the wall-clock label */
    uint16_t schema_ver;
    uint16_t source_id;   /* which process produced it */
    uint16_t kind;        /* enum dsm_kind */
    uint16_t flags;       /* enum dsm_flag bits */
    int32_t  v[4];        /* fixed-point values; meaning depends on kind */
    uint32_t seq;         /* per-source counter: a gap means lost data */
    uint32_t crc32;       /* covers every byte before this field */
};

/* We write the struct's bytes straight to disk, so its layout IS the file
 * format. If an edit changes the layout, the build stops here instead of
 * the files quietly becoming unreadable. */
_Static_assert(sizeof(struct dsm_record) == 48,
               "dsm_record must be exactly 48 bytes");
_Static_assert(offsetof(struct dsm_record, crc32) == 44,
               "crc32 must be the last 4 bytes of the record");
_Static_assert(__BYTE_ORDER__ == __ORDER_LITTLE_ENDIAN__,
               "the on-disk format assumes a little-endian host");

void record_init(struct dsm_record *r, enum dsm_kind kind, uint16_t source_id);
void record_seal(struct dsm_record *r);
bool record_intact(const struct dsm_record *r);

#endif

# term-project (Dark Sky Monitor) — CS 370
# Every target does what its name says. CLAUDE.md treats a lying target as a bug.

CC := gcc

# _POSIX_C_SOURCE: with -std=c17, the Pi's glibc hides fsync, ftruncate, pread
# and clock_gettime unless this is defined, and -Werror then fails the build.
# macOS shows them anyway, so leaving this out would only break on the Pi.
CFLAGS := -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -g -O1 -Isrc -Itests \
          -D_POSIX_C_SOURCE=200809L
SANFLAGS := -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer

# Library code (no main). Each step adds its files here.
SRC  := src/common/crc32.c src/common/record.c src/store/store.c
TSRC := tests/test_main.c tests/test_crc32.c tests/test_record.c tests/test_store.c
HDR  := tests/check.h tests/suites.h src/common/crc32.h src/common/record.h \
        src/store/store.h

TESTBIN := build/test_all

## all: build the test binary
all: $(TESTBIN)

$(TESTBIN): $(SRC) $(TSRC) $(HDR)
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(SRC) $(TSRC) -o $@

## test: run every test suite
test: $(TESTBIN)
	./$(TESTBIN)

## asan: rebuild with AddressSanitizer + UBSan and run the tests
asan: CFLAGS += $(SANFLAGS)
asan: clean test

## memcheck: run the tests under valgrind (Linux/Pi only, not on macOS)
memcheck: all
	@if ! command -v valgrind >/dev/null 2>&1; then \
	    echo "make memcheck: valgrind not installed here (expected on macOS - run this on the Pi)."; \
	  else \
	    valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all --error-exitcode=1 ./$(TESTBIN); \
	  fi

## soakcheck: 1-hour miniature of the graded 48h soak
soakcheck:
	@echo "make soakcheck: not implemented yet - needs the supervisor and heartbeat logging."
	@echo "Per spec 3.4 this must exercise: startup, hourly heartbeat (liveness/RSS/event counts),"
	@echo "an injected fault with detect-degrade-recover, and an orderly shutdown."

## deploy: rsync the tree to the Pi. usage: make deploy PI=pi@hostname
deploy:
	@if [ -z "$(PI)" ]; then \
	    echo "usage: make deploy PI=pi@hostname"; exit 1; \
	  else \
	    rsync -av --exclude '.git' --exclude 'build' --exclude 'transcripts' ./ $(PI):~/term-project/; \
	  fi

## clean: remove build artifacts
clean:
	rm -rf build

## help: list targets
help:
	@grep -E '^## ' $(MAKEFILE_LIST) | sed 's/^## /  /'

.PHONY: all test asan memcheck soakcheck deploy clean help

# Record format, data rates, and IPC

Detail behind `DESIGN.md` § Architecture, § Mechanism mapping and § Storage and data. The record
and header layouts are **implemented** (`src/common/record.h`, `src/store/store.h`). Everything
marked *proposed* in the record sections (the kinds, flags, `source_id`s and payloads, which
nothing depends on yet) was proposed by Liam and **confirmed by Nick on 2026-10-28**. The IPC section is Liam's
(mechanism E). The IPC is designed but not implemented.

## Record: 48 bytes, little-endian (implemented)

| Offset | Size | Field | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 8 | `t_mono_ns` | `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`, for intervals |
| 8 | 8 | `t_real_ns` | `CLOCK_REALTIME`, the wall-clock label |
| 16 | 2 | `schema_ver` | `DSM_SCHEMA_VER` (1) |
| 18 | 2 | `source_id` | producing process (table below) |
| 20 | 2 | `kind` | record kind (table below) |
| 22 | 2 | `flags` | bit flags (table below) |
| 24 | 16 | `v[4]` | `int32` fixed-point values; meaning depends on `source_id` and `kind` |
| 40 | 4 | `seq` | per (source, run) counter |
| 44 | 4 | `crc32` | CRC-32/IEEE over bytes 0–43 |

The layout is enforced at compile time with `_Static_assert`. Rules: `record_init()` zeroes all
48 bytes first; `record_seal()` is called last; the store refuses unsealed records.

## Segment header: 24 bytes (implemented)

`magic "DSKY"` (4) · `schema_ver` (2) · `record_size` (2) · `created_real_ns` (8) · `reserved`
(4, always 0) · `crc32` over bytes 0–19 (4). On reopen, any mismatch means the file is refused
and left untouched.

## Kinds and flags

| `kind` | Value | | Flag | Bit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SAMPLE | 1 | | `VALID` | 0 |
| FEATURE | 2 | | `STALE` | 1 |
| STATE | 3 | | `SYNTHETIC` (all replayed or provoked data) | 2 |
| HEARTBEAT | 4 | | `CALIBRATING` (sensor warming up) | 3 |
| FAULT | 5 | | `CLOCK_UNSYNC` (*proposed*) | 4 |
| START (*proposed*) | 6 | | | |

0 is never a valid kind or `source_id`, so a zeroed record never looks real.

## Payloads (proposed)

| `source_id` | `kind` | `v[0]` | `v[1]` | `v[2]` | `v[3]` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 `skyd` | SAMPLE | TSL2591 CH0 count (full spectrum) | CH1 count (IR) | gain multiplier | integration, ms |
| 2 `cloudd` | SAMPLE | sky (object) temp, m°C | ambient (die) temp, m°C | 0 | 0 |
| 3 `envd` | SAMPLE | temperature, m°C | humidity, milli-%RH | pressure, Pa | 0 |
| 4 `fusiond` | FEATURE | feature id | value ×1000 | window, s | samples in window |
| 4 `fusiond` | STATE | state | rules fired (bitmask) | confidence ×1000 | 0 |
| 5 `dskyd` | HEARTBEAT | subject `source_id` | RSS, KiB | CPU time, ms | cumulative events |
| any (6 = `stored`) | FAULT | fault code | errno | consecutive count | 0 |
| any | START | run number (from `dskyd`) | 0 | 0 | 0 |

- **Raw counts, not lux,** for the TSL2591: lux means little at night-sky levels, and storing
  counts plus gain and integration time lets the brightness conversion be redone later.
- **MLX90614 in m°C:** its 0.02 K step is exactly 20 m°C (`m°C = raw × 20 − 273150`), so there
  is no rounding (datasheet scale, verify at bring-up).
- **FAULT vs. `!VALID`:** an I/O failure is a FAULT (the first one, then at most 1 per 60 s while
  it lasts); a successful read with an implausible value (saturated, MLX error bit) is a SAMPLE
  with `VALID` cleared.
- **`seq` per run:** each process start writes START with `seq` 0. A gap within a run is
  provable loss; the time between runs is the restart gap.

## Rate derivation (computed, not measured)

| Record | Rate | Records/day |
|---|---|---|
| `skyd` SAMPLE | 1 per 5 s | 17 280 |
| `cloudd` SAMPLE | 1 per 1 s | 86 400 |
| `envd` SAMPLE | 1 per 10 s | 8 640 |
| FEATURE | 4 per min | 5 760 |
| STATE | on change, ≥ 1 per 10 min | ≥ 144 |
| HEARTBEAT | 6 per h (5 children + `dskyd`) | 144 |
| FAULT, START | per event | ≈ 0 in steady state |
| **Total** | **≈ 1.37 rec/s** | **≈ 118 400 → 5.7 MB/day** |

- 180 days of raw data ≈ 1.0 GB, on a 16 GB card.
- `write()` every 10 s ≈ 13.7 records ≈ 660 B per call; `fsync()` 1440 per day.
- I2C transfers (planned read sequences; datasheet protocol, verify at bring-up): TSL2591 status
  + data = 2 per sample → 0.4/s; MLX90614 ambient + object = 2 → 2/s; BME280 trigger + burst = 2
  → 0.2/s. **≈ 2.6 transfers/s in total.**
- Buffer headroom: a 1024-slot ring holds 17 min of `cloudd`, 85 min of `skyd` and 170 min of
  `envd`; `fusiond`'s 4096-record buffer for `stored` holds ≈ 50 min.

## IPC (mechanism E)

### Sensor → `fusiond`: shared-memory rings

One single-producer/single-consumer ring per sensor daemon: 1024 slots × 48 B in POSIX shared
memory under `/dev/shm`, plus one shared semaphore that every producer posts and `fusiond` waits
on with a 1 s timeout. `dskyd` creates the shared memory before the fork and unlinks it on
orderly shutdown, so a ring outlives the restart of either side.

Chosen over sockets for **decoupled lifetimes, not speed** (1.3 rec/s is slow): samples keep
queuing while `fusiond` restarts, and a sensor never blocks on the hub.

**Invariants:**

1. **Publish after write:** fill slot `head % N` with an already-sealed record, *then* advance
   `head` with a release store. The reader acquire-loads `head` and reads only slots below it, so
   a producer `kill -9`'d mid-copy never exposes a half-written slot. The restarted producer
   reads `head` from shared memory and overwrites that same slot.
2. **CRC on read:** the reader copies the slot out and checks `record_intact()` before use. A
   torn slot (a bug, not the protocol) is counted and dropped, never trusted.
3. **Never overwrite unread:** the producer writes only while `head − tail < N`. When the ring is
   full, it drops the *new* sample and increments an overrun counter in the ring header; the
   `seq` gap proves the loss.
4. **Reader restart:** `tail` advances only after the record has been forwarded to `stored`. If
   `fusiond` is killed in between, the restarted `fusiond` re-sends that record. The duplicate
   has the same (source, run, seq) and is removed at query time.
5. **Lock-free across processes:** `_Static_assert(ATOMIC_INT_LOCK_FREE == 2)`, because a
   lock-based atomic would deadlock if a process died holding the lock. **Assumed, confirmed at
   build on the Pi** (64-bit ARM).

Edge cases: a producer killed between advancing `head` and posting the semaphore only delays
the record until the reader's next 1 s timeout.

### Other channels

| Channel | Kernel object | Rate | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fusiond` → `stored`, `dskyd` → `stored` | `AF_UNIX` `SOCK_SEQPACKET`, one 48-byte record per message | 1.37 rec/s; 6 rec/h | `stored` is the only writer. While it is down, `fusiond` buffers 4096 records (≈ 50 min), then drops the oldest and counts. **Proposed (Liam), confirmed (Nick) 2026-10-28** |
| `dsq` ↔ `fusiond` | `AF_UNIX` `SOCK_STREAM`, line-based request/response | on demand | `state`, `health`. `dsq` reads segments directly, read-only |
| `dskyd` ↔ each child | pipe (child holds the write end) + `SIGCHLD` | ≥ 1 B per 5 s | EOF = died; 20 s silent = hung → `SIGKILL` |
| all → log | stderr → journald | ≈ 6 lines/h steady + 1 per event | survives a `dskyd` crash |

### Supervision (`dskyd`)

- Runs under systemd with `Restart=on-failure`; children set `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG`, so they exit
  with it and a restarted `dskyd` starts a clean tree.
- After a crash: restart with 1 → 2 → 4 … 60 s backoff; 60 s of healthy running resets it.
- A sensor daemon that sees 3 consecutive failed reads exits with a distinct "sensor absent"
  code. `dskyd` marks it `DEAD` and re-probes every 60 s instead of restarting fast, so an
  unplugged sensor never causes a restart storm.
- 5 crashes within 300 s → `DEAD`, re-probe every 60 s; the rest of the system keeps running.
- Heartbeat: one HEARTBEAT per child within 60 s of start, then hourly. Contents: RSS and CPU
  time from `/proc/<pid>/statm` and `/stat`, plus cumulative events from the ring counters.
- Each child passes its run number in its START record (see `seq` above).
